 Before you pick the best NAS for a small business, settle what the box actually has to do, because a small office rarely needs raw speed. It needs shared folders that respect Windows or Active Directory permissions, backups of every laptop, snapshots that ransomware cannot delete, and an offsite copy that runs without anyone remembering it. Hardware that handles all four quietly for five years is the goal, and that narrows the field faster than any benchmark.
 Original content from computingforgeeks.com - post 172410 
 We shortlisted six small business NAS units for offices of roughly 5 to 50 people, from a budget 4-bay file server to a short-depth rackmount and a ZFS appliance with no license fees. Every price, spec and drive policy below was checked against the manufacturer’s pages and live Amazon listings in October 2026, and the business features (domain join, immutable snapshots, high availability, backup targets) come from each vendor’s own documentation rather than the marketing pages. That matters this year, because Synology changed its drive rules twice and the result is more nuanced than “the lock is gone”.
 Best NAS for small business: quick picks

 Best for Windows and AD offices Synology DS1825+ about $1,480 8 bays (18 with expansion), 8 GB ECC, PCIe slot for 10GbE or 25GbE 
 Best budget QNAP TS-464 about $640 AD, quotas and a PCIe slot at the lowest price here, plus a ZFS OS option 
 Most hardware for the money UGREEN DXP6800 Pro about $1,100 Core i5, two 10GbE ports, six bays, 3-year warranty 
 Best rackmount Synology RS1221+ about $1,650 Short-depth 2U, 8 bays, High Availability support, no drive lock 
 Best ZFS with no license fees TrueNAS Mini X+ about $2,160 direct 32 GB ECC, dual 10GBase-T, IPMI, snapshot holds included 
 Prices are Amazon US on October 1, 2026, and they are moving during the 2026 memory and drive shortage, so treat each as a band and check the live price before you order. Drives are not included in any of them.
 How we picked
 We started from what a 5 to 50 person office asks of its file server and worked backwards, which ruled out a lot of popular home NAS boxes. A pick needed a domain join or LDAP integration, snapshot protection, a route to offsite backup, a vendor warranty of at least a year, and an Amazon listing sold and shipped in the US at a sane price. We verified specs on each manufacturer’s spec page, confirmed the exact Amazon listing and stock on the day, and read at least one independent review per model (BizTech, ITdaily, ITPro, NASCompares, ServeTheHome or StorageReview).
 We did not have these six units in the lab, so we do not quote throughput numbers of our own for them. Where software behaviour matters, we lean on vendor documentation and on testing we have done: our TrueNAS vs Unraid lab run injected real corruption into a ZFS pool and watched TrueNAS repair it, which is the behaviour the Mini X+ pick relies on. We dropped several candidates: the Asustor Lockerstor Gen3 and the Synology DS1525+ were only sold by third-party resellers, the new Synology neo+ series ships with non-ECC memory and was only listed through Amazon Japan, and two-bay models fall below what an office needs.

 TrueNAS Mini X+ 5 + 2 SSD Atom C3758 8C 32 GB ECC (64 GB) 2x 10GBase-T + IPMI Snapshot holds (full admin can release) 1 year (3 optional) 
 Synology DS925+: best overall for most offices
 For an office of up to about 20 people that wants a file server it can forget about, the DS925+ is where we would start, mostly because of the software around it rather than the box itself:
 Synology DS925+: Ryzen V1500B, 4 GB ECC, 4 bays plus 2 M.2, dual 2.5GbE. Image: Synology. 
 DSM joins an Active Directory domain or Microsoft Entra Domain Services from Control Panel, applies domain users and groups to shared-folder permissions, and supports Windows ACLs over SMB. Btrfs shared folders can take immutable snapshots, which Synology says “cannot be removed by any means” until a protection period you set expires (it recommends 7 to 14 days). That is the single most useful anti-ransomware control a small office can turn on. Hyper Backup then sends an encrypted, block-level incremental copy to another Synology, an rsync server, Azure, an S3-compatible bucket or Synology’s own C2 cloud. The spec page rates it for 40 concurrent SMB connections and 512 local users.
 It fits offices of 5 to 20 people that want domain-aware file shares, laptop backup and ransomware-resistant snapshots on one box. Look elsewhere if you need 10GbE, because there is no PCIe slot and therefore no upgrade path, or if your workload needs more than the 4 GB it ships with (plan an upgrade for Synology Drive, Active Backup or VMs, and note Synology limits warranty support on non-Synology RAM). NVMe storage pools still require Synology SSDs. It is about $760 on Amazon, sold by Amazon itself; check the live price .
 Synology DS1825+: best for Windows and Active Directory shops
 Once an office grows past 20 people, or its data clearly will not fit in four bays within a couple of years, we would step up to the DS1825+ rather than buying a second small box. It runs the same DSM business stack as the DS925+ on eight bays, with 8 GB of ECC memory and a PCIe slot:
 Synology DS1825+: 8 bays (18 with expansion), 8 GB ECC, PCIe Gen3 slot for 10GbE or 25GbE. Image: Synology. 
 The slot is a Gen3 x8 connector with a x4 link, enough for a 10GbE or 25GbE card, and two DX525 expansion units take it to 18 drives. BizTech ran one as the primary file and backup server for a 10-person office for a month, and called out that Active Backup for Business does not charge per seat, which is a real cost advantage over per-device backup software. Synology rates it for 60 concurrent SMB connections and 1,024 local users, and it is on Synology’s list of models that support WriteOnce (WORM) shared folders as well as immutable snapshots.
 We would buy it for a Windows office of 20 to 50 users with a domain controller, or for anyone who wants room to grow without a migration later. It is the wrong box if you want to run VMs or heavier apps on the NAS, because the 2018-era V1500B has no integrated graphics and modest headroom, or if you would rely on the expansion units for performance (NASCompares found the DX525 link runs at USB 3.2 Gen 1 speed, 5 Gbps). It is about $1,480 on Amazon, sold by Amazon itself; check the live price .
 QNAP TS-464: best budget small business NAS
 The TS-464 is the cheapest box here that still checks the business boxes, and it is the only budget pick with a PCIe slot. At about $640 it undercuts the DS925+ by over $100:
 QNAP TS-464: Celeron N5095, 8 GB, 4 bays plus 2 M.2, dual 2.5GbE, PCIe slot. Image: QNAP. 
 QNAP’s QTS handles Active Directory membership, Windows ACLs, and user, group and folder quotas, and it snapshots volumes on a schedule as often as every five minutes. The PCIe Gen3 x2 slot takes a 5GbE or 10GbE card later. The bigger option is the operating system: the TS-464 can run QuTS hero, QNAP’s ZFS-based OS, which adds WORM shared folders and immutable snapshots. You have to choose at install time, because switching from QTS to QuTS hero later erases the drives and QNAP requires removing them first, and inline deduplication on QuTS hero wants at least 16 GB.
 For an office of 5 to 15 people on a tight budget that still wants domain integration and a 10GbE path, it’s the obvious pick. Pass on it if you need ECC memory or more than 16 GB, which is this model’s ceiling, or fast NVMe storage (its M.2 slots run at Gen3 x1). It had 257 reviews and sells for about $640, now through a third-party seller (STC Distributors) rather than Amazon, and it currently ships on a later date; check the live price and ship date .
 UGREEN DXP6800 Pro: most hardware for the money
 On paper, nothing else here comes close for the price: a 10-core Core i5-1235U, two 10GbE ports, six bays, two Thunderbolt 4 ports, a PCIe x4 slot and a 3-year warranty for about $1,100. It’s the box we’d pick for a creative studio that moves large files over 10GbE all day:
 UGREEN NASync DXP6800 Pro: Core i5-1235U, 2x 10GbE, 6 bays, 3-year warranty. Image: UGREEN. 
 The catch is the software, and for a business it is a serious one. UGOS Pro has an Active Directory option in its UI, but an independent test of UGOS found it behaves as an LDAP bind rather than a true domain-member join, so test it against your own domain controller before rolling it out (that test used FreeIPA, not Windows Server). UGREEN’s own backup guide says its locked snapshots “remain manageable by an administrator, so they are not immutable recovery copies”, which means a compromised admin account can delete them. UGREEN also advertises “ODECC”, which is DDR5’s on-die error correction, not ECC memory.
 The right buyer is a small studio or team that cares most about 10GbE throughput, or an IT-comfortable office that plans to install TrueNAS on it (UGREEN has said, according to NASCompares, that a third-party OS does not void the hardware warranty as long as it does not damage the hardware). Avoid it if you depend on domain membership, need immutable snapshots for compliance, or want vendor support for the whole stack. We compared it in depth against its closest rival in ZimaCube 2 vs UGREEN DXP6800 ; it’s about $1,100 on Amazon, check the live price .
 Synology RS1221+: best rackmount NAS for a server closet
 If the office already has a rack, the RS1221+ is the one we would put in it, and its age is part of the reason. It is a short-depth 2U chassis with eight bays, expandable to 12 with an RX418 unit, running the same V1500B and DSM as the desktop Plus models:
 Synology RackStation RS1221+: short-depth 2U, 8 bays, 4x 1GbE, PCIe slot, High Availability capable. Image: Synology. 
 Because it launched before 2025, Synology’s newer drive rules do not apply to it, so third-party hard drives work for new pools. Its 2026 successor, the RS1226+, and the 4-bay RS826+ both state “Compatible drives are mandatory” on their spec pages. It supports Synology High Availability, which pairs two identical units for automatic failover, and Synology rates it for 180 concurrent SMB connections. Pairing has strict conditions, though: identical models running the same DSM version with the same number of LAN ports, identical drives in identical slots, and no SHR or M.2 SSD pools on the active server.
 It belongs in an office with a rack, a closet away from desks, and a plan to add 10GbE through the PCIe slot. Keep it out of the room if people sit nearby (ITPro measured the redundant-PSU RS1221RP+ at 58.7 dB at one metre), or if you will not buy a 10GbE card from Synology’s compatibility list (ITPro’s unit refused to boot with a Broadcom card and only worked with an Intel one). Out of the box it is 4x 1GbE. It’s about $1,650 on Amazon, and the dual-PSU RS1221RP+ is about $2,150; check the live price . On a smaller budget, QNAP’s 1U TS-464eU costs about $850 but has no PCIe slot and no 10GbE path.
 TrueNAS Mini X+: best ZFS appliance with no license fees
 For data where silent corruption is unacceptable (accounting archives, legal files, design masters), we’d choose ZFS on ECC memory, and the Mini X+ is the turnkey way to get it from the company that makes TrueNAS:
 TrueNAS Mini X+: Atom C3758, 32 GB ECC, 5+2 hot-swap bays, 2x 10GBase-T, IPMI. Image: iXsystems. 
 It ships with 32 GB of ECC memory (64 GB maximum), five hot-swap 3.5-inch bays and two 2.5-inch SSD bays, dual 10GBase-T and a dedicated IPMI port for remote management. The software is TrueNAS Community Edition, whose feature list includes Active Directory, LDAP, SMB multichannel, SMB auditing, “unlimited and immutable snapshots”, replication and cloud sync, with no per-user or per-feature license. Those snapshots cannot be edited, but a full administrator can still delete them, so TrueNAS recommends running daily work under its Sharing Admin role, which can place a snapshot hold but cannot release one. When we corrupted a gigabyte of one disk in a RAIDZ1 pool on a TrueNAS VM in our lab, TrueNAS served every file intact and a scrub repaired 108 MB in 48 seconds. If AD is the plan, our guide to joining TrueNAS to Active Directory covers the setup.
 Choose it when data integrity comes first and someone on the team is comfortable with ZFS concepts. Think twice if you need vendor-grade support, because the default warranty is one year (three is optional), or modern CPU performance, since the Atom C3758 dates to 2017. High Availability is only in TrueNAS Enterprise, not on the Mini. The Amazon listing TrueNAS runs is currently unavailable, so buy it direct: the diskless Mini X+ with the one year warranty is about $2,160 in the TrueNAS configurator , where you can also add the three year warranty or order it with drives fitted. The alternative is TrueNAS on hardware you choose, which our DIY NAS vs prebuilt breakdown prices out.
 Synology’s drive policy in 2026: what changed and what did not
 This is the question most small business buyers ask first, and the honest answer depends on the model. In 2025, Synology required drives from its own compatibility list on new Plus models. In October 2025, DSM 7.3 relaxed that for 2025 DiskStation Plus models like the DS925+ and DS1825+: third-party hard drives and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs can now create new storage pools. Two restrictions remain, and DSM 7.4 added a third. M.2 NVMe drives still have to be on Synology’s list for storage pools and cache. The 2025 and 2026 RackStation Plus models still require listed hard drives for new pools. DSM 7.4, released in June 2026, added hard-drive deduplication and compression that only works with Synology drives.
 Synology’s knowledge base also states the new policies “do not apply retroactively to previously launched systems”, and that clause is the reason the 2021 RS1221+ makes a better rack pick today than its successor. In practice this means a DS925+ or DS1825+ can take the same WD Red Plus or Seagate IronWolf drives you would put in any NAS. Our NAS hard drive picks cover which ones are CMR.
 What to look for in a small business NAS
 Directory integration that really joins the domain. If your users log in to Windows with domain accounts, the NAS should join that domain so permissions follow people rather than shared passwords. DSM, QTS and TrueNAS all do this; test UGOS before you depend on it.
 Snapshots that an admin cannot delete. QNAP warns that ransomware often goes after backups and snapshots first, using stolen admin credentials. Vendors use the word “immutable” for two different things, so check which one you are buying. Synology’s immutable snapshots and QNAP’s on QuTS hero cannot be deleted by anyone, admins included, until the protection period ends. TrueNAS snapshot holds stop day-to-day admins from deleting a snapshot, but a full administrator can release the hold. UGREEN’s locked snapshots stay deletable by any admin. Only the three Synology picks give you admin-proof snapshots out of the box; the TS-464 gets them once you switch it to QuTS hero.
 An offsite copy that runs itself. A NAS in the office is not a backup of the office. Schedule a nightly copy to a second NAS at another site or an S3-compatible bucket, and test a restore every quarter. Hyper Backup, QNAP’s HBS 3 and TrueNAS Cloud Sync all handle this.
 ECC memory where the data matters. The three Synology picks and the TrueNAS Mini ship with ECC; the QNAP TS-464 and the UGREEN don’t. For ZFS in particular, ECC guards against one of the few failure paths ZFS can’t catch itself: a bit flip in RAM before the checksum is calculated.
 A path to 10GbE, even if you do not need it today. Video editing over the network and full-machine backups are the first workloads to outgrow 2.5GbE. A PCIe slot (DS1825+, TS-464, RS1221+) or onboard 10GbE (DXP6800 Pro, Mini X+) keeps the box useful for its whole life, provided the switch can follow; our 10GbE managed switch picks cover that side.
 Warranty and support you will actually use. Three years is standard for Synology, QNAP and UGREEN’s 6-bay line, extendable to five on Synology in North America and Europe. TrueNAS Mini is one year unless you pay for three.
 Pairs with Best NAS for Jellyfin and Plex (2026): QuickSync Picks 
 TrueNAS or Unraid on a Mini PC (2026): Best DIY NAS Boxes 
 Best NAS Case (2026): Mini-ITX to 12-Bay TrueNAS Chassis 
 Hardening the NAS before the office depends on it
 The box matters less than how it is configured on day one, and a few settings decide whether a ransomware incident is a bad afternoon or a lost year. This is the checklist we would run on any of the six before moving the office’s data onto it:
 Create a named admin account with two-factor authentication, then disable or rename the default admin. Day-to-day users never get admin rights.
 Protect every shared folder with snapshots on a 7 to 14 day protection period, hourly or daily. On Synology, turn on immutable snapshots. On QNAP, run QuTS hero and use immutable snapshots or WORM in Compliance mode. On TrueNAS, give daily admins the Sharing Admin role so they can place holds but not remove them. On the UGREEN, replicate to a second box with separate credentials.
 Set the minimum SMB protocol to SMB2 or later, and keep the admin web interface off the internet. Use a VPN or the vendor’s relay service for remote access instead of port forwarding.
 Configure the offsite backup job on day one and restore one folder from it to prove it works.
 Connect a UPS over USB so the NAS shuts down cleanly on a power cut; our UPS picks for a NAS cover sizing.
 Enable email alerts for drive health, failed logins and snapshot or backup failures, and send them to a shared mailbox rather than one person.
 Done in that order, the NAS that costs $640 and the one that costs $2,160 can give a small office the thing that matters most: a copy of yesterday’s files that an attacker can’t delete before you need it. On the Synology picks, and on the TS-464 under QuTS hero, that holds even if the attacker has the admin password. On TrueNAS, it depends on keeping the full administrator account out of daily use.

 For teams of 2–20 people, a business-grade NAS handles shared file access, automated workstation backups, and local redundancy — without the per-user cost of cloud storage services.
 Cloud storage is convenient, but per-seat pricing adds up fast for a small team. A business NAS sits on your local network and gives every workstation a shared drive, automated backup, and a place to store project files — all without a monthly per-user fee. The right NAS for a small business is not just a consumer device with more bays. It needs to handle concurrent user access, integrate with existing user account systems, and keep running without attention for weeks at a time.
 This guide focuses on NAS devices that make genuine sense for teams of 2–20 people: models with strong multi-user performance, free business backup software, 10GbE upgrade paths, and the reliability features — ECC RAM, enterprise-grade drive certification, and proper RAID — that a business environment demands.

 Business NAS vs Consumer NAS: What Actually Differs
 The gap between a consumer NAS and a business NAS is not just marketing. Several technical differences matter when multiple people are accessing the same device simultaneously and the cost of downtime is real.
 ECC RAM is the most important differentiator that rarely gets attention on spec sheets. Consumer NAS devices almost universally use non-ECC RAM. ECC memory detects and corrects single-bit errors before they propagate to storage. In a ZFS-based or business-grade file system, a RAM error can silently corrupt data in ways that only become apparent months later. The Synology DS1522+ and DS923+ both support ECC DDR4 SO-DIMMs — a meaningful advantage for any environment where data integrity matters.
 24/7 drive certification is the second major difference. Consumer NAS drives like WD Red and Seagate IronWolf are rated for 24/7 operation, but the enterprise variants — WD Red Pro, Seagate IronWolf Pro — carry higher workload ratings (300 TB/year vs 180 TB/year) and longer warranties. A business NAS running under heavier concurrent load should use drives matched to that workload.
 Multi-user access control in business NAS platforms goes beyond simple password protection. Synology DSM and QNAP QTS both support per-user quotas, per-shared-folder permissions, audit logging of file access, and integration with existing directory services. Consumer NAS setups rarely need this complexity; business deployments often require it from day one.
 SMB/AD integration and support contracts round out the business-grade distinction. Synology and QNAP both offer professional support options for business deployments, something consumer-oriented platforms like TerraMaster are still building out.
 User Accounts, Permissions, and Active Directory Integration
 A small business NAS needs to handle user access properly from the start. There are two main approaches: local user accounts managed directly on the NAS, or joining the NAS to an existing Windows Active Directory domain.
 For teams without a Windows Server, local user accounts on the NAS are the practical choice. Both Synology DSM and QNAP QTS let you create user accounts, assign them to groups, and set per-shared-folder permissions — read-only, read/write, or no access — at the group or individual level. This works well for teams up to about 10–15 users before the management overhead becomes significant.
 For businesses already running Windows Server with Active Directory, joining the NAS to the domain means employees log into shared folders with their existing network credentials. No separate NAS password to manage. Synology DSM supports AD join via Control Panel > Domain/LDAP, and once joined, AD users and groups appear directly in the shared folder permission editor. QNAP QTS offers the same capability. The NAS does not need to be a domain controller — it simply joins the existing domain as a member server.
 Synology also offers Synology Directory Server, a Samba-based AD-compatible directory service that runs directly on the NAS. This lets a business run an AD-equivalent setup without a separate Windows Server license — practical for very small offices that want centralized user management without the infrastructure overhead.
 Automated Workstation Backup: Synology Active Backup and QNAP NetBak
 One of the strongest arguments for a business NAS over cloud storage for workstation backup is cost. Cloud backup at $5–10 per workstation per month adds up across a team. Synology Active Backup for Business is a free package available to any Synology NAS. It installs a lightweight agent on Windows, macOS, and Linux workstations, and backs them up to the NAS on a schedule — incremental after the first full backup, with deduplication across all protected machines.
 The Active Backup console shows the backup status of every protected workstation in a single view. You can set retention policies to keep daily backups for 30 days, weekly for 3 months, and monthly for a year — all stored efficiently on the NAS using deduplication. Restores can be done file-by-file or as a full bare-metal restore from the console.
 QNAP's equivalent is NetBak Replicator for Windows and the broader Hybrid Backup Sync (HBS3) platform. HBS3 handles workstation backup, NAS-to-NAS replication, and NAS-to-cloud sync (AWS, Azure, Backblaze B2, and others) from a single management interface. For businesses that want to replicate NAS data offsite automatically, QNAP's HBS3 is particularly well-integrated.
 TerraMaster's TerraBackup handles workstation backup for Windows and macOS, though the feature set and polish is currently behind Synology's Active Backup. For most small businesses, the Synology ecosystem's backup tooling is the primary reason to choose Synology over alternatives at similar price points.
 10 Gigabit Ethernet for Business NAS: When to Upgrade
 Standard gigabit Ethernet caps real-world throughput at roughly 100–115 MB/s. For light office use — opening documents, saving spreadsheets, occasional large file transfers — gigabit is adequate. But when multiple users are accessing the NAS simultaneously, that shared 1G pipe becomes the bottleneck.
 Consider the math: five users each doing sequential file transfers would theoretically each get 20 MB/s of throughput on a gigabit NAS. In practice, seek times, file system overhead, and drive throughput mean the real sharing is worse. With 10GbE, the theoretical ceiling is 1,000 MB/s — enough that the drives and CPU become the bottleneck rather than the network.
 The Synology DS1522+, DS923+, QNAP TS-664, and TS-464 all support 10GbE via PCIe expansion cards. Synology's E10G22-T1-Mini (one 10GbE port) and E10G18-T1 cards are compatible with the DS1522+ and DS923+. QNAP's QXG-10G1T card works with the TS-664 and TS-464.
 The upgrade to 10GbE also requires a 10GbE switch and 10GbE NICs in the workstations that will benefit. For small offices, a 10GbE switch with 4–8 ports costs $200–$400, and many recent desktop CPUs include integrated 2.5GbE at minimum. The realistic recommendation for most small businesses: start with 2.5GbE built-in (QNAP TS-664) or 1GbE (Synology), and add 10GbE only when multiple users regularly hit the ceiling simultaneously.
 Business Continuity: RAID, UPS, and Offsite Replication
 A business NAS that goes down takes the whole team's shared storage with it. Business continuity planning for a NAS has three layers: drive redundancy via RAID, power protection via UPS, and offsite replication for disaster recovery.
 RAID for business NAS: A 4-bay business NAS should run RAID 5 at minimum — three drives of usable capacity with one drive as parity, surviving any single drive failure. A 5- or 6-bay NAS should use RAID 6, which survives any two simultaneous drive failures. RAID 6 matters more when drives are large (16TB+) and rebuild times stretch to 24–48 hours — during which a RAID 5 array is fully vulnerable to a second failure destroying all data.
 UPS for NAS protection: Power outages and surges are the most common cause of NAS file system corruption. A UPS gives the NAS time to complete writes and shut down gracefully when power fails. Both Synology and QNAP support USB-connected UPS monitoring — the NAS polls the UPS status and initiates a controlled shutdown when the battery reaches a threshold. A basic 650VA UPS costs $60–$100 and is one of the highest-value additions to any business NAS setup.
 Offsite replication: RAID protects against drive failure but not against fire, theft, flood, or ransomware. Synology C2 Storage offers NAS-to-cloud replication directly from DSM. Backblaze B2 and Wasabi are compatible with both Synology (via Hyper Backup) and QNAP (via HBS3). A 1 TB/month offsite backup plan costs roughly $5–7/month depending on the provider — a modest premium for genuine disaster recovery capability.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 How many simultaneous users can a small business NAS support?
 It depends heavily on the workload. A 4-bay Synology like the DS923+ can comfortably handle 5–10 users doing light file access and backups over gigabit Ethernet. Heavier simultaneous workloads — video editing, large file transfers, or more users — benefit from 10GbE networking and a faster CPU like the AMD Ryzen R1600. The NAS itself rarely maxes out before the network does on gigabit connections.
 Does a business NAS require ECC RAM?
 ECC (Error-Correcting Code) RAM detects and corrects single-bit memory errors before they can corrupt data silently. For business use where data integrity matters, ECC is strongly recommended. Silent data corruption in RAM can write corrupted data to disk in ways that are not caught until weeks later. The Synology DS1522+ and DS923+ both support ECC DDR4, as do several QNAP business models. Non-ECC NAS devices are not disqualified for light business use, but ECC becomes more important as the amount of data and number of users grows.
 Can I join a Synology NAS to Windows Active Directory?
 Yes. Synology DSM supports joining an existing Windows Active Directory domain via Control Panel > Domain/LDAP. Once joined, AD users and groups appear in DSM and can be assigned permissions to shared folders just like local accounts — employees log in with their existing network credentials. Synology also offers its own Synology Directory Server package that runs an AD-compatible directory service directly on the NAS, useful for businesses that want centralized user management without a separate Windows Server license.
 What is the difference between RAID 5 and RAID 6 for business?
 RAID 5 can survive one simultaneous drive failure and uses one drive's worth of capacity for parity. RAID 6 uses two drives for parity and can survive two simultaneous drive failures. This distinction matters most on 5+ bay arrays where a rebuild after one failure takes 24–48 hours for large drives — during which a second failure would destroy the entire array. For business NAS with 5 or more bays, RAID 6 is the safer choice despite the additional capacity cost.

Best NAS for Small Business 2026: Synology, UGREEN & UniFi Compared | iFeeltech 
 Skip to main content 
 Key Takeaway
 Three vendors stand out in this comparison of the small business NAS market in 2026: Synology for software reliability, UGREEN for hardware value, and UniFi for ecosystem integration. QNAP's 2026 lineup is also worth considering for VM and Docker-heavy environments. Each has distinct strengths and trade-offs worth understanding before you buy.
 This guide is for offices of roughly 5–25 people that need shared file storage, endpoint backup, and local disaster recovery—and have someone on staff (or on contract) who can manage the hardware.
 RAID Is Not Backup
 RAID can keep a NAS available through one or more drive failures, depending on the RAID level. It does not protect against deletion, ransomware, theft, fire, or complete system failure. Every NAS deployment in this guide should include an offsite backup destination. See our 3-2-1 backup rule guide for implementation steps. Our RAID levels guide compares RAID 0, 1, 5, 6, 10 and SHR for a business NAS.
 Affiliate Disclosure: This article contains affiliate links. If you make a purchase through these links, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.
 If you're deciding between a NAS and a full server, our decision guide works through the criteria before you start comparing hardware.
 The small business NAS market has shifted considerably. UGREEN now ships newer Intel silicon and 10GbE at price points comparable to Synology's 2018-era Ryzen lineup, while Ubiquiti's UniFi UNAS line has introduced a new option for IT-managed offices.
 The Cheat Sheet (prices checked July 13, 2026) :
 Profile Best Pick Price 
 Software-first, reliability matters Synology DS925+ ~$720 
 Best hardware value, can tolerate software quirks UGREEN DXP4800 Plus ~$650–730 
 Already in UniFi ecosystem, have rack space UniFi UNAS Pro 8 $799 
 Which NAS Should Your Business Buy?
 Your Situation Best Choice Why 
 Prioritize software polish and reliability Synology DS925+ (~$720) DSM provides the most mature and predictable management experience in this comparison 
 Need 10GbE and best hardware value UGREEN DXP4800 Plus (~$650–730) More capable hardware for a similar price 
 Already running UniFi infrastructure, need 1U rack UniFi UNAS Pro 4 ($499) 1U, dual 10G SFP+, NVMe caching, license-free 
 Already running UniFi infrastructure, need 8 bays or redundant power UniFi UNAS Pro 8 ($799) 8 bays, dual redundant PSUs, native 10GbE RJ45 
 Creative/video team, need Thunderbolt UGREEN DXP6800 Pro (~$1,020–1,200) Dual 10GbE + Thunderbolt 4, Core i5 
 Small office, no server closet, want UniFi UNAS 4 ($379) Desktop form factor, quiet operation 
 Need ZFS, VMs, or Docker-heavy workloads QNAP TVS-h877AX (~$3,000+) ZFS + Ryzen 5 PRO (Zen 4); enterprise-grade, IT-managed environments 
 When not to buy a NAS: If your organization lacks internal IT support, depends entirely on cloud collaboration (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365), or cannot commit to maintaining offsite backups, a managed cloud storage solution may be more appropriate than on-premises hardware. Not sure whether a NAS, a cloud drive, or encrypted storage fits your workflow? Our guide to where business files should actually live works through the decision before you choose a product.
 How We Evaluated These Systems
 Our recommendations draw on direct deployment experience across client sites, supplemented by manufacturer specifications and independent testing where noted.
 Systems tested in-house: Synology DS925+, UGREEN DXP4800 Plus, UniFi UNAS Pro 4, UNAS Pro 8, UNAS 4
 Firmware versions: DSM 7.2 and 7.3; UGOS PRO 1.x; UniFi Drive 3.x and 4.x
 Drives used: WD Red Plus (CMR), Seagate IronWolf; RAID 5 and SHR configurations
 Network environment: 2.5GbE and 10GbE links; UniFi switches; Windows, macOS, and Linux clients
 Workloads tested: SMB file sharing, Time Machine backup, Active Backup for Business, Docker containers, Plex transcoding
 QNAP and TrueNAS sections are based on manufacturer specifications and published reviews; we have not deployed these specific 2026 models at client sites
 Prices verified: July 13, 2026, from manufacturer stores, Amazon, and B&H Photo
 Where a claim reflects our direct experience, we say so. Where it reflects manufacturer specifications, we identify the source. Editorial assessments are our own.
 Synology DS925+ Business Storage Capabilities
 Synology's 4-bay flagship delivers the strongest NAS software in our assessment, with trade-offs in processor generation and expansion options.
 Price: ~$720 (checked July 2026) | Bays: 4 (expandable to 9) | Networking: Dual 2.5GbE
 DiskStation Manager is, in our assessment, the strongest NAS operating system available for small business use—with an extensive app ecosystem, thorough documentation, and the broadest third-party integration support of any platform in this comparison.
 Hardware Specifications: 
 The DS925+ runs on AMD's Ryzen Embedded V1500B—a quad-core processor from AMD's 2018-era Ryzen Embedded platform. For straightforward file sharing and backup, it performs adequately. Compared to the Intel Pentium Gold 8505 in UGREEN's lineup, the V1500B is a generation behind:
 No integrated GPU or Intel Quick Sync acceleration (the processor is less suitable for frequent software transcoding)
 Slower performance for Docker containers and virtual machines
 Official power figures: 37.91W during access, 12.33W in HDD hibernation (based on manufacturer specifications)
 Synology also removed the PCIe expansion slot from the DS925+. Unlike the older DS923+, you cannot add a 10GbE card later. If you need 10GbE, the dual 2.5GbE ports can provide up to 5Gbps of aggregate bandwidth across multiple connections, but a single file transfer normally uses one 2.5GbE link unless SMB Multichannel is enabled and supported by both the NAS and client. For native 10GbE, you need to step up to the DS1525+.
 Where Synology Excels: 
 DSM software: The backup solutions , photo management, and surveillance apps are the strongest option in our assessment
 Synology Hybrid RAID (SHR): Unlike standard RAID, SHR lets you mix drive sizes and expand storage without wiping drives—ideal for businesses that add capacity gradually
 QuickConnect + Tailscale: Easy remote access without complex VPN setup
 Long-term support: Synology has historically provided long DSM update cycles across multiple hardware generations; established VAR channels for enterprise support
 Drive Compatibility (DSM 7.3+)
 DSM 7.3 restored broader third-party HDD and 2.5-inch SATA SSD support on 2025 Plus models—third-party drives now work with only a warning message. However, M.2 NVMe storage pool support, technical-support scope, and compatibility status still vary by model. Check Synology's current drive compatibility policy for your specific configuration.
 Growth Path: Expansion Support
 Among the three primary systems reviewed here, the DS925+ is the only 4-bay model with a first-party multi-bay expansion unit. The DX525 adds 5 more bays, scaling to 9 drives total. UGREEN and UniFi currently require a new chassis for more capacity.
 The Verdict
 Best for businesses prioritizing software stability over hardware specs. The aging CPU limits transcoding and VM performance.
 For a deeper look at Synology's ecosystem, see our comprehensive Synology NAS business guide .
 Check Synology DS925+ Price 
 UGREEN DXP4800 Plus Hardware and Value Proposition
 The DXP4800 Plus offers more processing power and connectivity per dollar than any other 4-bay NAS in this comparison, including built-in 10GbE networking.
 Price: ~$650–730 (checked July 2026) | Bays: 4 | Networking: 1× 10GbE + 1× 2.5GbE
 For roughly the same price as the DS925+, UGREEN ships a newer Intel processor, DDR5 memory, and 10GbE connectivity without add-on cards.
 What Sets It Apart: 
 Intel Pentium Gold 8505: A Q1 2022 hybrid architecture (one performance core, four efficiency cores) with Intel Quick Sync—capable of hardware-accelerated video transcoding that the V1500B cannot match
 Built-in 10GbE: No add-on cards needed; the second 2.5GbE port enables network segmentation
 8GB DDR5 RAM: Expandable to 64GB for memory-intensive workloads
 No drive restrictions: UGREEN explicitly supports third-party drives
 Why M.2 Slots Matter: 
 The two NVMe slots enable SSD caching, which can reduce latency in suitable random-I/O workloads—particularly when multiple users access frequently-used files simultaneously. Benefits vary by working set, RAID configuration, and application.
 Official Power Consumption: 
 UGREEN publishes 42.36W during drive access and 18.12W in hibernation. These figures are not directly comparable to the DS925+'s 37.91W/12.33W because drive configurations, measurement conditions, and processor architectures differ. The newer Intel platform offers stronger general compute performance and Quick Sync acceleration, but the published power figures do not support a direct performance-per-watt comparison.
 Where UGREEN Falls Short: 
 UGOS PRO is functional but noticeably less polished than DSM. The app ecosystem is smaller, documentation is thinner, and some enterprise features (like advanced snapshot management) are still in development.
 Support & Warranty: 
 UGREEN provides a two-year warranty and sells direct through their NAS store as well as Amazon and Newegg. However, UGREEN does not publish the type of enterprise support and advance-replacement SLA available through parts of Synology's channel. For businesses with strict compliance requirements (HIPAA, localized data sovereignty), UGREEN's newer entry into the market may require deeper security vetting compared to Synology's longer track record.
 The Verdict
 Best tested hardware-per-dollar in this comparison. Shorter support track record and smaller software ecosystem are the trade-offs.
 Newer UGREEN Option: DXP4800 Pro
 The DXP4800 Pro upgrades to an Intel Core i3-1315U (6-core/8-thread, up to 4.5 GHz) and supports up to 96GB of DDR5 memory while retaining 10GbE and 2.5GbE networking. UGREEN lists it at approximately $720. We have not tested this model yet, but businesses planning heavier virtual-machine or Docker workloads should compare it with the DXP4800 Plus before purchasing.
 For a detailed comparison, see our UGREEN vs Synology NAS analysis .
 Check UGREEN DXP4800 Plus Price 
 UniFi UNAS Pro 8 Rackmount Storage for UniFi Environments
 The UNAS Pro 8 delivers eight hot-swap bays and triple 10GbE connectivity at a price point typically reserved for 4-bay NAS systems.
 Price: $799 (MSRP via Ubiquiti Store) | Bays: 8 | Networking: 2× 10G SFP+ + 10G RJ45
 Third-party retailers like CDW and B&H may charge $830–$960 due to demand markups. Purchase directly from the Ubiquiti Store to secure the $799 MSRP. For IT-managed offices already running UniFi switches, access points, and Protect cameras, the UNAS Pro 8 consolidates storage management into a single platform.
 The Hardware: 
 Eight 3.5" bays plus two internal M.2 NVMe slots
 16GB RAM
 Three 10GbE ports (two SFP+, one RJ45)
 2× 550W hot-swap redundant PSUs
 2U rackmount form factor
 UniFi Ecosystem Integration: 
 UniFi OS consolidates storage, network, and camera management into a single interface. A UNAS is its own UniFi console and can be managed locally—it does not depend on a separate Network controller remaining online. Site Manager centralizes access across consoles, but each UNAS appliance operates independently.
 Noise: This Is Not a Desktop NAS
 The UNAS Pro 8 is enterprise rackmount hardware. In our deployments, the cooling fans were too noticeable for occupied office environments. This unit belongs in a server closet, IT room, or dedicated rack. For quiet desktop use, see the UNAS 4 below.
 Software Maturity in 2026: 
 UniFi Drive has progressed significantly since launch. As of mid-2026, documented capabilities include: SMB/NFS file sharing, Active Directory integration, snapshots, user groups, multiple RAID groups with hot-spare options, file encryption, local and remote backup (UNAS-to-UNAS, CIFS), and cloud backup to Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, Amazon S3, Backblaze B2, and Wasabi.
 It is still fair to say that UniFi Drive has a smaller application ecosystem and a shorter operational track record than Synology DSM. It lacks native SaaS backup for Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, and its snapshot capabilities are not yet comparable to Synology's immutable WORM-protected snapshots. But the gap has narrowed—verify current feature availability against your specific requirements rather than relying on early-launch assessments.
 Support and Replacement Options: 
 Ubiquiti provides a two-year warranty on products purchased directly from the Ubiquiti Store (one year through authorized resellers). UI Care extends eligible products to five-year coverage with advance replacement shipment and priority handling. This is a meaningful improvement, though it is not necessarily an NBD SLA comparable to Synology's enterprise support contracts.
 The Desktop Option — UNAS 4: 
 The UNAS 4 ($379, 4-bay, 2.5GbE, M.2 NVMe slots, desktop form factor) launched in early 2026 and was listed as available when checked July 13, 2026. It fills the gap for smaller UniFi offices that need a quiet, rackmount-free option. See our UNAS 2 vs UNAS 4 review for deployment guidance on both desktop models.
 The Verdict
 Strong bay-per-dollar value for UniFi shops with proper rack space. Not suitable for quiet office environments.
 For setup guidance, see our complete UniFi NAS business guide . If you're comparing the UNAS 4, Pro 4, and Pro 8 head-to-head, see our detailed UNAS model comparison .
 Check UniFi UNAS Pro 8 Price at Ubiquiti Store 
 Storage Sizing and Capacity Planning
 Calculating usable NAS capacity requires accounting for RAID overhead, filesystem formatting, snapshot reserves, and the difference between advertised TB and operating-system-reported TiB (a 10 TB drive shows roughly 9.09 TiB in the OS).
 Common RAID capacity formulas (equal-sized drives):
 RAID Level Usable Capacity Minimum Drives 
 RAID 1 1 drive's capacity 2 
 RAID 5 (drives − 1) × drive size 3 
 RAID 6 (drives − 2) × drive size 4 
 RAID 10 ~50% of raw capacity 4 
 SHR/SHR-2 Varies by drive sizes 2+ / 3+ 
 Current Data Recommended Config Usable Space 
 2–5 TB 4× 4TB (RAID 5) ~12 TB 
 5–15 TB 4× 8TB (RAID 5) ~24 TB 
 15–40 TB 6× 12TB (RAID 6) ~48 TB 
 A more complete capacity formula: current data + expected annual growth + retention requirements + snapshot overhead + 20–30% operating headroom. "Plan for twice your current data" is a useful shorthand, but insufficient for businesses with regulatory retention requirements or heavy snapshot use.
 Not Sure What You Need?
 Capacity planning is where most businesses get tripped up—RAID overhead, future growth, and drive selection add up quickly. If you're unsure whether you need 20TB or 50TB, or which platform fits your workflow, we can help.
 Schedule a 10-Minute NAS Sizing Call 
 Total Cost of Ownership: What You'll Actually Spend

 Additional costs to budget for: replacement-drive reserve, offsite backup storage or cloud egress charges, support contracts where required, and rack or shelf hardware for rackmount units.
 The DS925+ connects at 2.5GbE and benefits from a multigigabit or 10GbE switch in mixed network environments, even though it cannot use a 10GbE endpoint itself.
 Choosing the Right NAS Drives
 When purchasing NAS drives, verify that every drive uses CMR (Conventional Magnetic Recording) technology. Device-managed SMR (Shingled Magnetic Recording) drives can perform poorly during sustained RAID writes and rebuilds, increasing rebuild time and operational risk.
 Commonly suitable CMR NAS lines: WD Red Plus, WD Red Pro, Seagate IronWolf, Seagate IronWolf Pro, Toshiba N300.
 Models requiring verification: Some WD Red models use SMR—verify the exact model number and recording technology before purchase. Standard Seagate Barracuda drives and any drive whose spec sheet does not explicitly state "CMR" or "PMR" should also be checked against the current manufacturer specification. Our NAS hard drive guide compares specific WD Red and Seagate IronWolf models by capacity, power and noise.
 Manufacturers have historically changed recording technology within the same product line without updating model numbers. Always verify the specific SKU against current spec sheets before purchasing.
 Power Consumption Comparison
 For NAS units running 24/7, power draw affects operating costs. These figures come from manufacturer specifications and are not directly comparable across vendors—test methodologies, drive configurations, and measurement conditions differ.
 Metric Synology DS925+ UGREEN DXP4800 Plus UniFi UNAS Pro 8 
 Drive access (mfr. spec) 37.91W 42.36W 250W max; typical not published 
 HDD hibernation (mfr. spec) 12.33W 18.12W N/A 
 At $0.13/kWh, a continuous 12W difference costs approximately $14 per year (roughly $41 over three years). The UNAS Pro 8's 250W figure includes a 225W maximum drive-power budget and is not a typical operating measurement—treat cross-vendor power comparisons as directional rather than precise.
 UPS and Graceful Shutdown
 Every NAS deployment should include an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) with USB or network signaling for graceful shutdown. Synology and UGREEN support automated safe shutdown with compatible UPS hardware. For UniFi NAS deployments, verify UPS compatibility and test shutdown and power-restoration behavior with the current UniFi Drive and UPS firmware. A power loss during active writes or a RAID rebuild can leave incomplete writes or array inconsistencies. A UPS reduces this risk, but it does not replace an independent backup.
 The 3-2-1 Backup Rule
 Follow the industry standard: 3 copies of your data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite. A NAS may hold your primary data or serve as one backup destination, but RAID does not count as a separate backup copy. Maintain two independent backups, including one offsite—such as iDrive, Backblaze B2, or AWS Glacier. Our complete 3-2-1 backup rule guide walks through implementation step by step. Choosing the offsite service? Our iDrive vs Acronis Cyber Protect comparison breaks down cost and features for small-business backup.
 Get iDrive Business Backup 
 NAS Security and Business Continuity Compared
 Data protection and disaster recovery capabilities vary significantly across these three platforms. This table reflects documented features as of July 2026.
 Capability Synology UGREEN UniFi 
 Identity integration Local users, AD/LDAP, MFA (Secure SignIn) Local users, basic MFA (TOTP) Local users, AD integration, MFA (UniFi Identity)

 Support & warranty 3-year standard; NBD replacement on eligible products with paid enterprise support contract 2-year warranty; consumer support channels 2 years (direct from Ubiquiti); 1 year (authorized resellers); UI Care extends to 5 years with advance replacement

 Key distinctions: 
 Synology's immutable snapshots (WriteOnce/WORM) provide tamper-proof recovery points that standard Btrfs or UniFi snapshots do not. An immutable snapshot and a standard snapshot serve different security functions.
 Synology's NBD replacement applies only to eligible products under a paid enterprise support contract—it is not a default feature of every Synology purchase.
 UniFi's cloud backup destinations are native to UniFi Drive but do not include SaaS backup for Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace mailboxes and documents.
 UniFi Protect now supports selected ONVIF-compatible third-party cameras without per-camera licensing, in addition to native UniFi cameras.
 Other Systems Worth Considering: QNAP and TrueNAS
 QNAP's 2026 Lineup
 QNAP's 2026 Ryzen and QuTS hero refresh deserves consideration for more demanding workloads. The TVS-h877AX, TVS-h1277AX, and TVS-h1677AX run AMD Ryzen 5 PRO 7645 processors (Zen 4 architecture, 6-core/12-thread, up to 5.1 GHz) with QuTS hero and the ZFS file system.
 What ZFS adds: ZFS provides data integrity verification through checksumming, self-healing capabilities (when valid redundant data is available for repair), inline compression, and deduplication. ZFS deduplication can require substantial memory and may reduce write performance depending on the workload—it should not be enabled without evaluating the memory and performance impact for your dataset. Synology's Btrfs provides comparable data integrity features through checksumming and snapshots, though the implementations differ in scope and approach.
 QuTS hero h6.0 introduces dual-NAS high availability— active-passive failover between two NAS units, where the standby system takes over when the active system fails. This is enterprise-grade functionality at a price point within reach for larger small businesses.
 The caveat: these are enterprise-class systems priced accordingly (the TVS-h877AX starts above $3,000 diskless). QNAP's setup is also more complex than Synology DSM. The dual-OS architecture (QTS vs. QuTS hero) and extensive configuration options make it better suited to environments with dedicated IT management.
 The TrueNAS Alternative
 For teams comfortable with Linux and ZFS, the TrueNAS Mini X+ from iXsystems offers a turnkey ZFS appliance with 5+2 hot-swap bays, an octa-core Intel C3758, 32GB ECC DDR4, and dual 10GbE—backed by enterprise support. Pricing is configuration-dependent; contact iXsystems for current quotes.
 TrueNAS Community Edition has no software licensing fee, although supported appliances, enterprise features, and professional support have separate costs. TrueNAS SCALE can run on any x86-64 hardware, giving budget-conscious IT teams ZFS-grade data integrity, native Docker support, and no recurring software fees. The trade-off is a steeper learning curve and the absence of polished mobile apps.

 Is the Synology DS925+ worth buying in 2026?
 For straightforward file storage and backup, the DS925+ remains a solid choice thanks to Synology's mature software. However, the AMD V1500B is a 2018-era Ryzen Embedded processor—the processor is less suitable for frequent software transcoding, heavy Docker workloads, and virtualization. If those matter to you, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus offers more capable hardware at a similar price point.
 Can I upgrade the DS925+ to 10GbE later?
 No. The DS925+ has no supported 10GbE network upgrade option. Dual 2.5GbE can provide up to 5Gbps of aggregate bandwidth across multiple connections, but a single transfer normally remains limited to one 2.5GbE link unless SMB Multichannel is enabled and supported by both the NAS and client. If 10GbE is on your roadmap, consider the DS1525+ or the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus, which includes 10GbE out of the box.
 Is UGREEN's software reliable enough for business use?
 UGOS PRO handles the essentials: file sharing, user management, Docker, and media streaming. But it's noticeably less polished than Synology's DSM. Documentation is thinner, the app ecosystem is smaller, and you'll occasionally hit rough edges. If you're comfortable troubleshooting or have IT support, it's fine. For hands-off operation, Synology is still the safer choice.
 Is the UniFi UNAS Pro 8 too loud for an office?
 Yes, unless you have a dedicated server closet or IT room. The UNAS Pro 8 is a 2U rackmount with enterprise-grade cooling fans—in our deployments, it was too noticeable for occupied office space. It belongs in a rack, not under a desk. The UNAS 4 ($379), a quiet desktop 4-bay option, launched in early 2026 and was listed as available when checked July 13, 2026. The UNAS 2 ($199) remains a good choice if you need an even smaller footprint.
 Which NAS offers the best value in 2026?
 The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus delivers the most hardware per dollar: Intel Pentium Gold 8505, 8GB DDR5, and built-in 10GbE for around $650–730. By comparison, the DS925+ (approximately $720) ships with a 2018-era CPU and no 10GbE upgrade path.
 Should I use a NAS or cloud storage for my business?
 Both. A NAS can provide local access and control over storage, but drives, backup, electricity, maintenance, and administration remain costs. Privacy depends on access controls, applications, and any external services. Cloud storage provides offsite redundancy for disaster recovery. The practical approach: use your NAS for active data and script nightly backups to offsite cloud backup such as iDrive or Backblaze B2. For help deciding which combination fits your business, see where your business files should actually live . For a full breakdown of cloud options, see our best cloud storage for small business comparison.
 Should small businesses consider QNAP in 2026?
 QNAP is worth evaluating if your team needs ZFS-based storage, advanced virtualization, or Docker-heavy workloads. New 2026 models like the TVS-h877AX feature AMD Ryzen 5 PRO 7645 processors (Zen 4 architecture, 6-core/12-thread) with strong multi-core performance and QuTS hero's ZFS file system. These are enterprise-class systems priced accordingly—the TVS-h877AX starts above $3,000 diskless. The trade-off: QNAP's dual-OS environment (QTS and QuTS hero) is more complex to configure than Synology DSM. For straightforward file storage and backup at a lower budget, Synology or UGREEN are easier to deploy and operate day-to-day.
 What does 'AI NAS' actually mean for a small business?
 AI NAS marketing commonly refers to photo organization, semantic search, external AI integrations, or security analytics; availability varies by platform and model. Running a local LLM (private ChatGPT equivalent) on the NAS benefits significantly from dedicated NPU or GPU hardware, though models can technically run on CPUs with limited performance. Synology AI Console connects supported applications to configured AI providers. Model-based name masking requires Container Manager and at least 8GB memory; predefined masking types have different requirements. Provider processing and usage charges may apply, and masking is not guaranteed to remove all sensitive data. Check Synology's technical requirements for the exact model and feature.
 AI capabilities vary considerably by platform, application, and model. Some systems provide photo classification, external AI-service integrations, or security analytics, while local language-model performance depends heavily on available CPU, GPU, memory, and software support. For most small businesses, backup reliability, restore testing, security controls, networking, and vendor support remain more important selection criteria than AI branding.

 5 Criteria to Look For Before Buying a NAS for Small Business
 Key buying criteria so you get the right fit the first time.
 Remember every listed NAS here is diskless, budget drives separately
 The price shown for a NAS enclosure covers the hardware chassis, CPU, and RAM only, not the actual storage drives, NAS-grade drives built for 24/7 operation like Seagate IronWolf or WD Red still need to be budgeted on top, often adding $80 to $200 or more per bay depending on capacity and drive type.

 This matters more the more the NAS will do beyond simple file storage, like Plex transcoding or running multiple docker containers, less if it's purely a basic backup target.
 Check the specific CPU model and RAM amount (and whether RAM is upgradeable) rather than choosing primarily by bay count.
 Understand RAID as a rebuild-time safety net, not a substitute for real backup
 RAID configurations protect against a single drive failure by letting the array rebuild from redundant data, but RAID is not a backup, it does nothing to protect against accidental deletion, ransomware, theft, fire, or a controller failure that affects the whole array at once.
 This distinction matters because treating RAID redundancy as sufficient backup protection is a common and genuinely risky misunderstanding, a real backup strategy needs a copy of critical data stored somewhere physically separate from the NAS itself.

 Match drive type (HDD vs SSD/NVMe) to your actual access pattern
 Traditional hard drives offer the lowest cost per terabyte for bulk storage like media libraries or backups, while SSD or NVMe-based NAS storage costs significantly more per terabyte but delivers much faster random access speeds, genuinely useful for frequently-accessed files, active project work, or serving as a fast cache tier.

 Consider noise level if the NAS will run continuously in a shared living or office space

 Frequently Asked Questions
 How many concurrent users can a small business NAS handle on gigabit Ethernet?
 A standard 1GbE connection works fine for document-heavy work with under 5 simultaneous users, but throughput per person drops noticeably once more people are transferring large files at the same time. Upgrading to 2.5GbE or 10GbE, on both the NAS and a matching switch, multiplies per-user throughput for larger or media-heavy teams.
 Do I need Active Directory integration for a small business NAS?
 Most small businesses eventually migrate from individual NAS logins to centralized directory sync as the team grows past roughly 5 users. It's genuinely useful for managing accounts at scale, but the setup is complex enough that it usually needs IT help to configure correctly the first time.

 Yes. Most guidance treats a NAS only as a backup destination for computers, but ransomware attacks specifically targeting NAS devices are increasing.  Do I really need a UPS for a business NAS?
 Yes, treat it as a required companion purchase. A power outage that hits mid-write can corrupt a RAID array, and a USB-connected UPS lets the NAS detect the outage and shut down safely before that happens.

Best NAS for Small Business Backup and File Storage (2026 Buyer's Guide) - IP Security Depot 
 Skip to main content 
 In this article 
 Quick Answer 
 The right small-business NAS is decided by bay count, network speed and where the box lives, not by brand. Pick enough bays to survive a parity rebuild, enough network to finish the backup window, and a chassis that fits the room you actually have.
 Best rack NAS for multi-user backup: Ubiquiti UNAS-PRO — seven 2.5/3.5-inch bays, 10G SFP+ uplink, 2U chassis.
 Best quiet desktop NAS for an office: QNAP HS-264-8G-US — fanless 2-bay, Intel Celeron N5105, dual 2.5GbE.
 Best all-flash NAS for shared project files: QNAP TBS-464-8G-US — four M.2 NVMe slots, dual 2.5GbE bondable to 5 Gbps.
 Best compact NAS for branch and UniFi sites: Ubiquiti UNAS-2-B — 2 bays, 2.5 GbE, runs entirely on PoE++.
 Best offsite rotation target: QNAP TR-002-US — 2-bay hardware-RAID enclosure over USB 3.2 Gen 2 at 10Gbps.
 Best capacity expansion when the NAS is full: QNAP TL-D1600S-US — sixteen SATA bays in a desktop JBOD shelf.
 This guide is for the person who owns IT at a company with ten to a hundred seats: the office manager who inherited a file share, the integrator adding a backup target next to a recorder, the MSP standardizing branch storage. It covers the network storage we stock and ship today, the capacity and bandwidth math that decides which one fits, and the difference between a snapshot and a backup — a distinction that costs people their data every year. If your storage job is video retention rather than files, start with how to size NVR hard drives without guessing , then come back here. Everything below is in the network attached storage category.
 Start With the Workload, Not the Bay Count
 Bay count is the first number everyone asks about and the last one that should drive the decision. Three very different jobs get called "NAS," and they stress the hardware in opposite directions.
 A backup target. Write-heavy, almost entirely sequential, read only during a restore or a test. It needs capacity and parity far more than it needs CPU. The failure mode that matters is a second drive dying during a rebuild, so bay count is really a redundancy decision, not a capacity one.
 An active file share. Twenty people opening, saving and searching documents all day is random I/O with bursty concurrency. Here the processor, the memory ceiling and the network interface decide whether the share feels instant or feels like 2009. Spinning disks handle it; flash handles it better.
 A continuous ingest archive. Camera streams and log pipelines write around the clock and never stop to let a rebuild finish. Sustained write throughput and drive class matter more than peak numbers, and the box needs to be sized so that a degraded array still keeps up.
 Why it matters. A fanless two-bay unit is an excellent file share for a quiet office and a poor primary backup target for a company with real retention requirements. A seven-bay rack unit is the opposite. Buying one chassis to do all three jobs is how small businesses end up with a single point of failure holding both the live data and its only copy.
 How We Picked
 We limited the field to network and direct-attached storage sitting in our warehouse today, then shortlisted on the criteria that change an install outcome rather than a spec sheet:
 Enough bays for the parity scheme you actually need. Two bays means RAID 1 and a 50% capacity tax. Four or more opens RAID 5; six or more makes RAID 6 sensible, which is the first configuration that survives a second failure during a rebuild. Bay count sets your risk floor.
 A network port faster than gigabit. Gigabit Ethernet tops out around 110 MB/s in practice, and that single number has stretched more backup windows past sunrise than any drive. Every pick here runs 2.5GbE or faster, because the uplink is usually the bottleneck long before the disks are.
 A form factor that fits the room. Rack units need depth, airflow and a cabinet. Desktop units need a surface, quiet operation and a nearby outlet. One pick here needs no outlet at all. Placement kills more deployments than performance does.
 An honest growth path. Storage demand only moves one direction. We favored units that can take mixed-capacity drives, bond links, or attach an expansion shelf, so phase two is not a forklift replacement.
 Ubiquiti UNAS-PRO — Best Rack NAS for Multi-User Backup and File Storage
 Drive bays: 7, 2.5-inch or 3.5-inch, mixed capacities supported · Network: (1) 10G SFP+, 10G/1G · RAID: 5 or 6 parity schemes · OS: UniFi OS · Power: AC/DC input, 160W · Dimensions: 442.4 × 325 × 87.4 mm · Form: 2U rack-mount, standard 19-inch
 Seven bays is the number that makes this unit worth racking. It is the point where RAID 6 stops feeling expensive — you give up two drives to parity and still keep five working for you, which means a drive can fail, and a second can fail mid-rebuild, without the array going with it. The 10G SFP+ uplink removes the gigabit ceiling that defines most small-business backup windows, turning a multi-hour nightly job into something that finishes before anyone notices. Two honest trade-offs. First, that is one network port, not two, so there is no link redundancy and you need an available SFP+ port or transceiver on the switch; plan the uplink before the unit arrives. Second, UniFi OS is a different philosophy from the app-store-driven NAS operating systems — provisioning and access control flow from the UniFi console you may already run, which is clean if you live in that ecosystem and limiting if your plan depends on third-party packages. Verify that before you commit.

 Not every storage decision happens in a server room. When the NAS has to live in a conference room, a reception closet or an AV rack ten feet from someone's desk, acoustic output is the spec that makes or breaks the placement, and this chassis has none — no fan, nothing to fail mechanically on the cooling side. The N5105's four cores handle indexing, a backup job and media transcoding at the same time without the stalls older dual-core units hit, and dual 2.5GbE means the share is not throttled to gigabit the moment two people copy large files. The trade-offs are structural, not flaws. Passive cooling means thermal headroom is the hard constraint, so it wants free air around it and not a stack of gear on top. The 8GB of memory is soldered, so a roadmap with multiple virtual machines on it should look elsewhere now rather than discover the ceiling later. And two bays means RAID 1, which is mirroring, not capacity.

 QNAP TBS-464-8G-US — Best All-Flash NAS for Shared Project Files
 Drive bays: 4 × M.2 2280 NVMe Gen3 x2, no SATA bottleneck · CPU: Intel Celeron N5105, 4-core / 4-thread, burst to 2.9 GHz, AES-NI · Memory: 8 GB DDR4, fixed · Network: dual 2.5GbE, bondable to 5 Gbps aggregate · Video: dual HDMI outputs · Form: all-flash desktop NASbook, no spinning drives
 This is the pick for teams whose complaint is latency, not capacity: design files, shared databases, virtual machine images, or any workload where a dozen people hammer the same folder and spinning disks spend their day seeking. Four NVMe slots on PCIe Gen3 x2 mean the drives are not the limit — bond both 2.5GbE ports to a capable switch for up to 5 Gbps and the network is still the ceiling, which is the right problem to have. AES-NI in the processor means volume encryption costs almost nothing in CPU, so encrypting a share holding client data is a decision you can make on the merits. The trade-off is cost per terabyte and the capacity ceiling that comes with it; flash is not where bulk archive belongs. Memory is fixed at 8 GB, so treat container and VM plans as a hard budget. The practical pattern is flash here for live work, parity disk elsewhere for retention.

 Multi-site organizations keep running into the same wall: each branch needs local storage, but nobody wants a separate NAS login and licensing scheme per location. This unit answers that narrowly and well. Storage policies, disk health alerts and retention schedules live in the same UniFi console as the cameras and switches, which means one dashboard for a dozen sites instead of a dozen logins. Running entirely on PoE++ from the included adapter is the underrated part: in a wall-mounted closet with one data drop and no spare receptacle, that is the difference between installing today and scheduling an electrician. At 2.85 lbs it mounts almost anywhere, and the USB-C port covers direct-attach backup or emergency recovery. Be clear-eyed about scope.  The third copy in a 3-2-1 plan has to leave the building, and for a small business that usually means a drive set that someone carries home or to a safe deposit box. This enclosure is the cleanest version of that: two 3.5-inch drives, hardware RAID handled by the enclosure's own microprocessor rather than the host, and a 10Gbps Type-C link so the weekly copy does not take a shift. Because parity runs on board, there is no driver stack to maintain and no host dependency on the array format. It also serves as plain capacity expansion for a NAS or workstation that has run out of internal bays. Three things to plan for. It is direct-attached, not networked, so it needs a host and is not a backup destination for the whole office on its own.  Every growing company eventually fills a NAS and faces the same choice: replace the platform, or add bays. Sixteen SATA slots in one shelf is the add-bays answer at a scale that actually buys several years — the right shape for footage archives, bulk file retention and backup targets where drive count matters more than peak speed. Because it is a JBOD shelf rather than a standalone appliance, it keeps your existing volumes, users and shares intact; growth becomes incremental instead of a weekend migration. The non-negotiable prerequisite: your host NAS must support SATA JBOD expansion and must list this unit, so confirm the model against QNAP's compatibility list before ordering, not after. It is also a desktop chassis, which means shelf or table space rather than rack units — convenient in a branch with no cabinet, awkward in a tidy server room.  Raw vs Usable: The Capacity and Backup-Window Math
 The capacity printed on a drive label is not what you get on the share, and the gap is bigger than most buyers expect. Three deductions stack, in this order.
 Parity. RAID 1 costs half. RAID 5 costs one drive. RAID 6 costs two. Take an illustrative array of six 8 TB drives: RAID 5 leaves five drives of data, or 40 TB raw usable; RAID 6 leaves four, or 32 TB.
 Binary accounting. Drives are sold in decimal terabytes, operating systems report binary tebibytes. Multiply by roughly 0.909. That 32 TB becomes about 29 TB as the file manager will show it.
 Free-space headroom. Keep 20% unallocated. Snapshots need room to retain changed blocks, and a filesystem running at 95% full slows down and complicates rebuilds. That 29 TB is now about 23 TB of real working capacity — 48% of the 48 TB you purchased. Plan from that number, and size for about 2.5 times today's data if the array has to last three to five years.
 The backup window. Throughput, not capacity, decides whether the job finishes. Gigabit Ethernet delivers roughly 110 MB/s in practice, so a 1 TB initial full backup takes about 2.5 hours. At 2.5GbE, call it 280 MB/s and a little over an hour. At 10 Gbps, roughly 1,100 MB/s, the same terabyte moves in about fifteen minutes. Nightly incrementals are small — a 3 TB dataset changing 2% a day is only 60 GB — but the initial seed, a monthly full, and especially a restore all run at full size. Size the link for the restore, because that is the day someone is standing over your shoulder.
 Rebuild time is the hidden risk. Resilvering a large array reads every remaining drive end to end while still serving clients, which can take a day or more and is precisely when a second drive is most likely to quit. That exposure is the whole argument for RAID 6 over RAID 5 on large disks, and it is why a degraded array should not also be absorbing peak write load. We covered the ugly version of this in why RAID rebuilds bring down the whole recorder .
 3-2-1, and why snapshots are not backups. Three copies of the data, on two different media, with one offsite. A NAS with parity is one copy. Snapshots are point-in-time views of that same array — superb for undoing a bad save or a crypto-locker that hit a share, worthless when the chassis is stolen, flooded, or the volume itself fails. Pair snapshots with a real replica: a second NAS at another site, a cloud target, or a rotating pair of drives in a direct-attached enclosure. And test a restore quarterly. An untested backup is a hypothesis.
 Installation and Operations
 Placement and airflow. Rack units pull air front to back and need clearance behind the cabinet, not just inside it; a NAS crammed against a wall in a closet with no ventilation runs hot, and drive life tracks temperature closely. Desktop units need clear space on all sides, and fanless designs especially need nothing stacked on them. Keep drives out of rooms that swing below freezing or above office temperature.
 Power. Every NAS belongs on a UPS. Not for uptime, but because an unexpected power loss during a write is how arrays get corrupted and rebuilds get started. Give the UPS enough runtime for a clean shutdown and enable the NAS's automatic shutdown on low battery. If the unit is PoE-powered, the switch feeding it becomes part of that calculation — the UPS has to cover the switch, not the storage.
 Cabling and uplinks. A 2.5GbE port needs Cat5e at minimum and will be happier on Cat6; a 10G SFP+ port needs a matching switch port plus a transceiver or DAC, which is the item most often missing on install day. Put storage traffic on its own VLAN so a backup job cannot starve voice or production traffic, as described in designing a network that doesn't compete with production traffic .
 Drives. Buy drives rated for continuous duty, not desktop drives. Spread purchases across two lots or vendors when you can, so a bad batch does not take two bays at once. Keep one cold spare on the shelf for every array; the day a drive fails is not the day to discover a two-week lead time.
 Management. Turn on SMART monitoring, schedule monthly scrubs, enable email or push alerts, and verify the alerts actually arrive by testing one. Change default credentials, keep the management interface off the public internet, and patch the NAS OS on the same schedule as your servers — network storage is a standing ransomware target precisely because it holds the backups.
 FAQ
 How many bays does a small business actually need? 
Four at minimum if the NAS holds anything you cannot recreate, because four bays make RAID 5 practical. Six or more if you want RAID 6 and the ability to survive a second failure during a rebuild. Two-bay units are excellent file shares and mirrors, but they are a thin foundation for primary backup.
 Is 2.5GbE enough, or should I go straight to 10GbE? 
For a file share serving fewer than about twenty users, 2.5GbE is a large upgrade over gigabit and needs no switch replacement if yours already has multi-gig ports. Go to 10 Gbps when a full backup or restore has to finish inside a tight window, or when several users move very large files at once.
 Do snapshots replace backups? 
No. Snapshots live on the same array as the data, so they recover deleted files, bad edits and ransomware-encrypted shares quickly, but they disappear with the chassis in a fire, theft or volume failure. Use snapshots for fast rollback and a separate offsite copy for disaster recovery.
 Rack or desktop? 
Rack if you already have a cabinet with depth, airflow and a UPS, and if the unit will be managed by IT rather than touched by staff. Desktop if the site has no cabinet, if the box must sit in occupied space where noise matters, or if a branch install has to go in with one data drop and no electrician.
 Can I mix drive capacities in one NAS? 
Some platforms allow it, including units that explicitly support mixed-capacity drives, but a traditional parity array sizes every member to the smallest drive, so a larger disk wastes the difference. Mixing is a reasonable way to use drives you already own; it is a poor way to buy a new array.
 What should I check before buying an expansion shelf? 
Confirm the host NAS supports expansion enclosures, confirm your exact model appears on the vendor's compatibility list, and confirm the required port and cable type are free on the host. Expansion support varies by model, and an unsupported shelf is an expensive paperweight.
