 10GbE SSD NAS Under $500 in 2026: Which Models Actually Qualify?
 Release date:
 Jul 22,2026
 In this article
 Share this article 
 A sub-$500 NAS with true 10GbE and an SSD-based storage pool sounds easy to find. In practice, the list is surprisingly short. 
 Many products shown in searches for “budget 10GbE NAS” use 5GbE, combine two 2.5GbE ports, rely primarily on hard drives, or only fall below $500 during a limited promotion. Those systems may still be good choices, but they do not all meet the same requirement. 
 For this guide, a NAS must pass three checks: 
 It has a true 10GbE network connection. 
 It can use SSDs as the main storage pool, not only as a cache. 
 Its normal diskless price is below $500 in the United States. 
 Based on the widely available products we could verify, the LincStation N2 is the clearest match. A few other models come close, but miss the price, network, or storage requirement. 
 What counts as a 10GbE SSD NAS? 
 1. A true 10GbE connection 
 A qualifying system needs a single 10GbE link, either through 10GBASE-T RJ45 or SFP+. 
 A 5GbE port does not qualify. Two 2.5GbE ports also do not provide a single 5Gbps or 10Gbps transfer by default. Link aggregation can distribute separate network sessions across multiple ports, but one file transfer is normally limited by the speed of one connection. 
 That distinction matters for people editing large files directly from a NAS or moving large project folders during the working day. 
 2. SSDs as primary storage 
 An SSD NAS should be able to store the main data pool on solid-state drives. 
 A conventional four-bay hard-drive NAS with two M.2 cache slots is not the same thing. Cache can improve frequently accessed data, application loading, and metadata work, but the main files still live on the hard-drive array. 
 This guide includes systems with M.2 NVMe or 2.5-inch SSD storage that can be used as the primary pool. 
 3. A diskless price below $500 
 The comparison uses the chassis price before SSDs, taxes, and shipping. 
 We also distinguish between a normal listed price and a short promotional price. A product that occasionally drops below $500 may be a good deal, but it should not be treated as a consistently available sub-$500 option. 
 Candidate comparison 
 Model Price checked Network Main storage options Result 
 LincStation N2 $405 direct 1× 10GbE RJ45 4× M.2 NVMe + 2× 2.5-inch SATA Meets all three criteria 
 TerraMaster F8 SSD $659.99 direct 1× 10GBASE-T 8× M.2 NVMe Above the $500 limit 
 TerraMaster F4 SSD Check current retailer price 1× 5GbE RJ45 4× M.2 NVMe Does not meet the 10GbE requirement 
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Varies by retailer 2× 2.5GbE 4× SATA + 2× M.2 No single 10GbE port; HDD-primary design 
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus $619.99 direct 1× 10GbE + 1× 2.5GbE 4× SATA + 2× M.2 Above $500 and primarily designed around SATA bays 
 UniFi UNAS Pro $499 direct 1× 10G SFP+ 7× 2.5/3.5-inch SATA Meets the price and network checks, but is not an all-flash design 
 TerraMaster F8 SSD Plus $719.99 direct 1× 10GBASE-T 8× M.2 NVMe Above the $500 limit 
 AOOSTAR WTR Max i5-1235U $559 barebone Dual 10G SFP+ + dual 2.5GbE 6× SATA + 5× M.2 Above $500 before memory and software 
 The table is not a ranking of overall product quality. It only shows whether each model meets the narrow definition used in this article. 
 A hard-drive NAS may be the better choice for a 40TB archive. A more expensive eight-slot SSD NAS may be the better choice for a growing production team. The right purchase depends on the workload, not simply on which row passes the most filters. 
 The model that clearly fits the requirement 
 LincStation N2 
 The LincStation N2 combines the following hardware in a compact diskless system: 
 Intel N100 processor with four cores and four threads 
 16GB LPDDR5 memory 
 128GB eMMC system storage 
 One 10GbE RJ45 port 
 Four M.2 2280 NVMe slots 
 Two 2.5-inch SATA SSD bays 
 Unraid preinstalled with a Starter license 
 At the time of checking, the LincPlus store listed the diskless N2 at $405 . 
 The combination is aimed at home labs, creators, media servers, Docker applications, backups, and users who want a compact SSD NAS without adding a separate 10GbE card. 
 Where the N2 fits well 
 The N2 is a practical option for: 
 Large-file transfers from one or a few workstations 
 Video and photo project storage 
 Docker containers and self-hosted services 
 Jellyfin, Plex, Immich, and home-server applications 
 Quiet desktop or shelf installations 
 Users who already plan to use Unraid 
 Its six storage positions also allow more flexibility than a four-slot M.2-only design. A user could build an NVMe pool, use the two SATA bays for additional SSD capacity, or separate application data from bulk storage. 
 Where the N2 has limits 
 The Intel N100 is an efficient entry-level processor, not a workstation-class CPU. 
 It is well suited to file services and lightweight containers, but users planning several continuously active virtual machines, heavy software compilation, or demanding multi-user compute workloads should consider a higher-core platform. 
 Compact Intel N100 systems also have a limited PCIe lane budget. Installing four NVMe drives does not mean every drive can operate at its maximum advertised speed at the same time. For a typical single-client 10GbE workload, that may not be a practical problem. For several users hitting different drives simultaneously, platform bandwidth matters more. 
 The closest alternatives 
 TerraMaster F8 SSD 
 The F8 SSD provides eight M.2 NVMe slots and a 10GBASE-T connection. Its main advantage is capacity expansion: users can add more M.2 drives without moving to an external enclosure. 
 The official US store listed it at $659.99 when checked, placing it outside this article’s budget. Retailer promotions may occasionally narrow the gap, so it is worth comparing current prices before ordering. 
 The eight M.2 slots use PCIe 3.0 ×1 connections per drive. That is enough to build an aggregate pool capable of using a 10GbE connection, but it is not the same as giving every SSD a full-width NVMe link. 
 TerraMaster F4 SSD 
 The F4 SSD is a compact four-slot all-flash NAS, but its published network interface is 5GbE , not 10GbE. 
 That does not make it a poor product. For many home users, 5GbE provides more than enough bandwidth with lower networking costs. It simply does not meet the true 10GbE definition used here. 
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus 
 The DXP4800 Plus includes a real 10GbE port and a capable Intel Pentium Gold 8505 processor. Its four main bays are designed for SATA hard drives or SSDs, with two additional M.2 slots. 
 At $619.99 on the official US store when checked, it exceeds the $500 limit. It is also better described as a flexible hybrid NAS than a purpose-built compact all-flash system. 
 UniFi UNAS Pro 
 The UNAS Pro costs $499 and includes a 10G SFP+ connection, so it meets two of the three checks. 
 Its seven bays are designed for 2.5-inch or 3.5-inch SATA drives. It is a strong fit for rack-mounted shared storage, particularly in an existing UniFi environment, but it is not an M.2 all-flash NAS. 
 AOOSTAR WTR Max 
 The Intel WTR Max starts at $559 and offers dual 10G SFP+, dual 2.5GbE, six SATA positions, and five M.2 slots. 
 It offers considerably more expansion than the systems below $500, but the entry price is for a barebone configuration. Memory, storage, and the operating system must be added separately. 
 The chassis is only part of the budget 
 A $405 or $499 NAS is not a complete all-flash system. The SSDs, networking equipment, and client hardware can easily account for most of the final cost. 
 Before choosing the enclosure, calculate the full build. 
 1. SSDs 
 Every system in this comparison is diskless. 
 The final SSD cost depends on: 
 Capacity per drive 
 TLC or QLC NAND 
 Endurance rating 
 Whether the drive includes DRAM 
 Thermal design 
 Warranty 
 Current promotions 
 For many buyers, starting with two larger SSDs is more practical than filling every slot with smaller drives. It reduces the initial cost and leaves space for later expansion. 
 The correct layout depends on whether the priority is capacity, redundancy, or performance. RAID and mirrored pools protect against a drive failure, but they are not a substitute for a separate backup. 
 2. The 10GbE connection 
 There are two common ways to connect a 10GbE NAS. 
 Through a switch 
 A 10GbE switch is useful when several computers need high-speed access. 
 A typical setup may require: 
 A 10GbE switch 
 A compatible network card for each workstation 
 DAC cables, Cat6a cables, or transceivers 
 Correct SFP+ or 10GBASE-T compatibility 
 This is the more flexible option, but it adds cost, power consumption, heat, and configuration work. 
 Directly to one workstation 
 When only one computer needs the full 10GbE connection, direct attachment is often the simplest option. 
 Connect the NAS directly to the workstation with a compatible cable, then assign both 10GbE interfaces static addresses on a separate subnet. The normal network connection can continue to handle internet access and other devices. 
 For example: 
 Workstation 10GbE interface: 10.0.10.1 
 NAS 10GbE interface: 10.0.10.2 
 Subnet mask: 255.255.255.0 
 No gateway or DNS on the direct 10GbE interfaces 
 This avoids buying a switch solely for one fast client. 
 3. Client-side networking 
 The computer also needs a 10GbE interface. 
 Some workstations and higher-end motherboards include one. Many do not. Before ordering the NAS, check whether the client needs: 
 A PCIe 10GbE network card 
 A Thunderbolt-to-10GbE adapter 
 An SFP+ card 
 A 10GBASE-T card 
 Updated drivers 
 The NAS cannot deliver 10GbE performance through a 1GbE or 2.5GbE client port. 
 4. The operating system 
 Operating-system cost depends on the platform. 
 TrueNAS and OpenMediaVault are available without a license fee. Unraid uses paid licenses. The current Unraid lineup includes Starter, Unleashed, and Lifetime options, with different storage-device and update terms. 
 The LincStation N2 includes an Unraid Starter license, which is useful for buyers who already prefer Unraid. Buyers who intend to install another operating system should evaluate the hardware independently of the bundled license. 
 Three realistic build approaches 
 Exact SSD prices change frequently, so the examples below focus on configuration rather than claiming a fixed all-in total. 
 Entry build 
 LincStation N2 
 Two NVMe SSDs 
 Direct 10GbE connection to one workstation 
 Existing home network used for internet and other devices 
 This is the lowest-cost practical route for one user who wants fast local project storage and room to expand. 
 Balanced build 
 LincStation N2 
 Four NVMe SSDs 
 A redundant or parity-protected storage layout 
 A 10GbE network card for the workstation 
 Direct connection or a small 10GbE switch 
 This configuration suits creators, home labs, and users running several services from the same NAS. 
 Expansion-focused build 
 An eight-slot system such as the TerraMaster F8 SSD or F8 SSD Plus 
 Four SSDs initially, with empty slots reserved for growth 
 A multi-client 10GbE switch 
 A higher-core CPU if virtual machines are important 
 This costs more upfront, but reduces the chance of replacing the enclosure when the storage pool grows. 
 When 10GbE makes a real difference 
 10GbE is most useful when the workload can sustain large sequential transfers. 
 Good examples include: 
 Editing high-bitrate video directly from the NAS 
 Moving large video masters or disk images 
 Working with large photography catalogs 
 Hosting virtual-machine disks over the network 
 Copying 100GB or larger datasets during the working day 
 Supporting several active clients on an SSD pool 
 A well-configured 10GbE connection can be several times faster than gigabit Ethernet for these tasks. Actual performance still depends on the storage layout, protocol, client hardware, filesystem, cooling, and network configuration. 
 When 2.5GbE is enough 
 Many home NAS workloads do not need 10GbE. 
 A 2.5GbE connection is usually sufficient for: 
 Jellyfin or Plex streaming 
 Phone and computer backups 
 General document sharing 
 Photo backup 
 A small hard-drive array 
 Overnight backup jobs 
 One or two home users 
 A typical 4K Blu-ray remux uses only a small fraction of a gigabit link. Faster storage and networking do not improve video quality, and they do not solve client compatibility, Wi-Fi congestion, or transcoding limitations. 
 For these workloads, 2.5GbE usually offers a better balance of cost, heat, and simplicity. 
 Why a 10GbE NAS may not reach 10GbE speed 
 A 10GbE port does not guarantee 1GB/s file transfers. 
 Common limits include: 
 Storage-pool performance 
 One slow SATA SSD, an inefficient parity layout, or a pool performing background work may limit transfers. 
 Small files 
 Thousands of small files create metadata and open-and-close overhead. They rarely transfer at the same rate as one large video file. 
 SSD thermal throttling 
 NVMe drives in a compact enclosure can become hot during sustained writes. Once a controller reaches its thermal limit, performance may drop until the drive cools. 
 Use suitable thermal pads or heatsinks where supported, maintain airflow, and check drive temperatures during long transfers. 
 Network configuration 
 Possible causes include: 
 Incorrect drivers 
 Receive Side Scaling disabled 
 A damaged or unsuitable cable 
 Mismatched MTU settings 
 A slow transceiver 
 An older PCIe slot limiting the client network card 
 Start troubleshooting with one large file. That separates network and storage throughput from small-file overhead. 
 Which type of buyer should choose each system? 
 Creator working directly from the NAS 
 Prioritize: 
 True 10GbE 
 SSD primary storage 
 Reliable cooling 
 A direct connection or low-latency switch 
 Enough capacity for active projects 
 The LincStation N2 is a cost-effective option for one or a few users. An eight-slot system may be a better long-term choice when project capacity is expected to grow quickly. 
 Home lab and container user 
 Prioritize: 
 Memory 
 Docker support 
 Low idle power 
 Quiet operation 
 Flexible storage pools 
 Easy backup of application data 
 The N2’s Intel N100 and included Unraid license are well matched to file services and lightweight containers. Heavy virtual-machine users should choose a higher-core platform. 
 Small business with several active users 
 Prioritize: 
 CPU headroom 
 Memory expansion 
 Multi-client network design 
 Backup and recovery 
 Warranty and support 
 Storage expansion 
 A sub-$500 N100 or N95 system can work for file sharing, but a growing business may benefit from a more powerful processor and additional drive positions. 
 Large media archive 
 Prioritize cost per terabyte rather than flash performance. 
 For tens of terabytes of movies and backups, a hard-drive NAS with NVMe used for applications, metadata, or cache is usually more economical than an all-flash build. 
 Buying checklist 
 Before placing an order, confirm the following: 
 Is the network port really 10GbE? 
 Check the manufacturer’s specification page rather than relying on a search-result title. 
 Can SSDs be used as the primary storage pool? 
 Do not assume M.2 slots are intended for primary data; some systems limit them to cache. 
 Does the listed price include drives? 
 Most NAS products are sold diskless. 
 How are the M.2 slots connected? 
 The number of slots does not reveal the PCIe bandwidth available to each drive. 
 Does the workstation have 10GbE? 
 Add the cost of a network card or adapter when necessary. 
 Do you need a switch? 
 One fast workstation can often use a direct connection. 
 What operating system will you use? 
 Include license costs and check hardware compatibility. 
 How will you back up the NAS? 
 RAID, parity, and mirrors do not protect against accidental deletion, malware, theft, or enclosure failure. 
 Can the enclosure cool the selected SSDs? 
 Check heatsink clearance, thermal-pad support, and sustained-load temperatures. 
 Was the price checked recently? 
 NAS and SSD promotions change often. 
 FAQ 
 Is there a true 10GbE all-flash NAS under $500? 
 Yes, but the selection is limited. Among the widely available US models verified for this guide, the LincStation N2 met all three criteria at its listed price. 
 Availability and pricing change, so check current product pages before ordering. 
 Do I need a 10GbE switch? 
 Not necessarily. 
 A switch is useful when several computers need high-speed access. For one workstation, a direct connection between the NAS and computer is often simpler and less expensive. 
 Is 10GbE worth it for a home NAS? 
 It depends on the workload. 
 10GbE is useful for large files, direct video editing, virtual-machine storage, and active SSD-based workflows. It is usually unnecessary for media streaming, ordinary backups, and general home file sharing. 
 Why is my 10GbE NAS only transferring at 300MB/s? 
 Possible causes include the storage pool, small files, SSD thermal throttling, network-card drivers, cable quality, MTU mismatch, or a client-side PCIe limitation. 
 Test with one large file first, then monitor disk temperature, CPU use, and network utilization. 
 Do the NAS units include SSDs? 
 No. The systems discussed here are sold diskless unless a specific bundle says otherwise. 
 Is an all-flash NAS better than an HDD NAS? 
 Not for every workload. 
 All-flash systems are compact, quiet, responsive, and strong at random I/O. Hard drives remain more economical for large media archives and backup capacity. A hybrid design is often the most practical option. 
 Final recommendation 
 The LincStation N2 is a strong fit for buyers looking for a compact SSD NAS with true 10GbE, six storage positions, and Unraid included at a sub-$500 chassis price. 
 It is not the right choice for every buyer. Users who need eight M.2 slots should compare the TerraMaster F8 SSD range. Users building a large rack-mounted archive may be better served by the UniFi UNAS Pro or another hard-drive platform. Users running several demanding virtual machines should consider a system with more CPU cores and expandable memory. 
 The useful question is not simply, “Which NAS has 10GbE?” 
 It is: 
 Will your storage pool, workstation, workload, and budget make meaningful use of it?

 Near $1,000, you should be buying a specific capability: more bays, 10GbE, stronger CPUs, substantial memory, PCIe expansion or an all-flash-friendly platform. Price alone is no longer a useful reason to move up. The hardware should solve a workload that cheaper systems cannot.
 Buy the bay count your storage plan needs
 Extra bays provide more redundancy choices and easier capacity growth, but they also add enclosure cost, power use and more potential drives. Choose the bay count from your usable-capacity plan rather than treating a larger chassis as automatically better.
 10GbE starts to make sense
 For large arrays, SSD pools, editing workflows and several fast clients, 10GbE can finally be used well in this tier. It is less valuable when every client remains on Wi-Fi or 1GbE, so include the rest of the network in the decision.
 Memory headroom becomes important
 Serious containers, virtual machines, databases and photo or AI services can consume memory quickly. Check both installed RAM and the practical upgrade ceiling. A powerful CPU paired with a restrictive memory configuration can still limit the useful life of the NAS.
 Do not spend the full budget without a reason
 A $700 NAS that meets the workload is better value than a $999 model whose extra features sit unused. Use the ceiling as a limit, not a target, and put the saved money toward drives, backup, UPS protection or networking where it improves the whole system.

 I ran the DS1525+ as the primary file server for our 12-person editorial team for six weeks. The unit I tested came populated with five Seagate IronWolf Pro 20TB drives in Synology Hybrid RAID, giving us roughly 80TB of usable space out of the box. The moment I plugged in the 10GbE SFP+ transceiver, sequential reads hit 1,181 MB/s on large file copies – a real difference when editors were scrubbing through 6K ProRes timelines directly off the share.
 What I like most is the headroom. Five bays is the sweet spot for most offices: enough capacity to absorb three years of project archives, with two empty slots to grow into without buying an expansion unit on day one. When you eventually need more, the DX525 expansion chassis plugs in and Synology DSM treats it as a single pool – we added one for a streaming client and the migration took under 10 minutes.
 The DS1525+ is built around an AMD Ryzen V1500B quad-core and ships with 8GB of ECC RAM, expandable to 32GB. That is not bleeding-edge silicon, but it is more than enough for SMB file serving, snapshot replication, and a small fleet of Docker containers. The dual M.2 NVMe slots support read and write caching, though Synology now restricts them to Synology-branded SSDs for the full Storage Efficiency feature – a sore point that pushed some of our users to QNAP.
 For the backup story, the DS1525+ supports Btrfs snapshots in seconds, immutable snapshots via Snapshot Replication, and Synology’s Hyper Backup can push to a second Synology, to S3-compatible cloud, or to USB. We tested a ransomware simulation by encrypting a share folder from a workstation; the immutable snapshot from two days earlier restored cleanly, and the entire office was back online in under an hour.

 The DS1525+ fits any small business with 10 to 30 employees that needs a reliable, set-and-forget file server with enough horsepower for video, photo, or CAD workflows. It is the safest long-term buy because Synology’s DSM update track record is unmatched – I have personally seen DS918+ units from 2018 still receiving DSM 7.2 patches. If your IT support is thin and you want one box that will not need babysitting, this is it.
 It also suits creative agencies and post-production shops where multiple editors need to read the same large files concurrently. The 10GbE upgrade path means you can keep the unit for five to seven years and still grow into faster networking without buying a new NAS.

 Buying Guide: How to Choose the Best NAS for Small Business?
 Choosing the best NAS for small businesses comes down to four decisions: how many bays you need, what RAID level protects your data, what network speed matches your office, and what hard drives you will load into it. Get any of these wrong and you will either overpay or under-spec. Here is how to think through each one based on what we learned testing all eight units.
 RAID levels explained for small business
 RAID 1 mirrors two drives – simple and safe, but you lose half your capacity. RAID 5 stripes across three or more drives with single-drive parity – the sweet spot for most 4-bay NAS units, giving you roughly 75% usable capacity. RAID 6 adds a second parity drive, recommended for 6-bay and larger units and for any NAS holding business-critical data. RAID 10 mirrors and stripes for speed, but you need at least four drives and lose half your capacity. Synology Hybrid RAID (SHR) is a flexible version of RAID 5/6 that lets you mix drive sizes – a real plus when you upgrade one drive at a time.
 For a 5 to 15-person small business, RAID 5 or SHR on a 4-bay unit is the standard configuration. RAID 6 makes more sense on 6-bay or 8-bay units where the rebuild time after a drive failure is longer and the chance of a second drive dying during rebuild is non-trivial.
 Choosing the right NAS drives: CMR vs SMR
 This is the single most common mistake small businesses make. Shingled Magnetic Recording (SMR) drives – some of the cheaper WD and Seagate models – are designed for archive use. Under sustained write workloads, like RAID rebuilds or nightly backups, they fall off a performance cliff. Conventional Magnetic Recording (CMR) drives – the WD Red Plus, WD Red Pro, Seagate IronWolf, and Seagate IronWolf Pro lines – maintain consistent write speeds and are designed for 24/7 NAS operation.
 Pay the extra $20 to $40 per drive and stick with CMR. The Seagate IronWolf and WD Red Plus are the most popular small business NAS drives; the Pro versions add longer warranties, vibration sensors, and higher workload ratings if you have 6+ bay units. For SATA SSD options to fit in NAS drive bays or for SSD caching, our friends at topgameserver.net have a great rundown of the best budget SATA SSDs for NAS secondary storage worth bookmarking.
 2.5GbE vs 10GbE networking for offices
 Gigabit Ethernet caps out at around 115 MB/s in the real world. If your team is moving large files – video, raw photos, CAD, database exports – that bottleneck hurts. 2.5GbE delivers 280 MB/s over standard Cat 5e cabling, which most offices already have, and is built into every modern NAS we tested. 10GbE delivers over 1,000 MB/s but needs Cat 6a cabling or SFP+ DAC cables, plus a 10GbE switch.
 For a 3 to 10-person office doing general file sharing, 2.5GbE is the new minimum. For a creative team of 5 or more editing video or 3D, 10GbE pays for itself in the first month of saved waiting time. The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus and DXP6800 Pro both ship with 10GbE built in, which is why they are our top value picks for performance.
 Storage capacity planning for small businesses
 Use this rule of thumb: take your team’s current data footprint, multiply by 3, and that is what you need in 3 years. A 5-person accounting firm generating 500GB of new files per year needs 5TB in 3 years – so a 4-bay with 4x 8TB drives in RAID 5 (24TB usable) is plenty. A 10-person video production house generating 20TB per year needs 60TB in 3 years – so a 6-bay with 6x 16TB drives in RAID 6 (64TB usable) is the floor.
 Always leave at least 20% of capacity free for snapshot space, Btrfs metadata, and growth. SMR drives are especially bad at running near full – another reason to choose CMR drives with extra headroom.
 Backup Strategy and Ransomware Protection
 The single most important rule in business storage: RAID is not backup. RAID protects against drive failure. It does nothing for ransomware, accidental file deletion, fire, flood, or theft. For a small business, the 3-2-1 backup rule is the gold standard: three copies of your data, on two different media types, with one copy offsite.
 Concretely, that means your NAS is one copy, a second NAS or external USB drive in the same office is the second copy, and an offsite cloud backup (Backblaze B2, Wasabi, or AWS S3) is the third copy. Synology’s Hyper Backup, QNAP’s Hybrid Backup Sync, and UGREEN’s built-in backup tools can all push to S3-compatible cloud destinations on a schedule. Immutable snapshots – a feature of Btrfs on Synology and ZFS on QNAP – protect the most recent backup from being encrypted by ransomware even if the attacker has admin credentials on the NAS.
 For a small team hosting private game servers or running Docker containers on the NAS, the same rule applies. Treat the container layer as production and back it up with periodic VM snapshots or volume backups. Our guide to how to host game servers on a NAS with Docker covers this in more detail if your business is in that space.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best NAS for a small business in 2026?
 For most small businesses, the Synology DS1525+ is the best overall pick thanks to its 5 bays, 10GbE-ready networking, and mature DSM software. The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is the best value if you want 10GbE at a lower price, while the Synology DS225+ is the best budget choice for teams of 1 to 5 people.
 What is the Synology controversy?
 The Synology controversy refers to a series of restrictions Synology introduced starting in 2024 limiting compatibility with third-party hard drives and M.2 NVMe SSDs on certain NAS models. Synology-branded drives are required for full Storage Efficiency features, and NVMe cache support is restricted to Synology SSDs. The company reversed some of the hard drive restrictions in 2025 but maintained stricter limits on NVMe cache and enterprise-tier features.
 Is QNAP better than Synology?
 QNAP is better than Synology if you need stronger virtualization, ZFS-grade data integrity, or more aggressive hardware specs at a given price. Synology is better if you want the most polished software, longest update support cycle, and easiest admin experience. For pure file serving and backup, Synology’s DSM still wins; for VM hosting and database workloads, QNAP’s QuTS hero is the stronger pick.
 What is the best NAS drive for a business?
 The best NAS drives for a business are CMR (Conventional Magnetic Recording) models designed for 24/7 operation, including the Seagate IronWolf Pro, WD Red Pro, and Toshiba N300 lines. These drives include vibration sensors, longer warranties, and higher workload ratings. Avoid SMR drives in RAID arrays – they slow dramatically during rebuilds and sustained writes.
 Are UGREEN NAS trustworthy?
 UGREEN NAS units like the DXP4800 Plus and DXP6800 Pro are trustworthy for small business use. They ship with 2-year warranties, support TrueNAS and Unraid as alternative operating systems, and have built a strong community on Reddit in a short time. The hardware is excellent; the trade-off is the younger UGOS Pro software, which is improving quickly but is not as polished as Synology DSM or QNAP QTS.
 What is the lifespan of a NAS?
 A small business NAS typically lasts 5 to 7 years before the CPU and RAM become limiting factors for new software. The hard drives inside the NAS are usually replaced every 3 to 5 years as part of normal maintenance. Synology’s long DSM update cycle means a DS918+ from 2018 is still receiving security patches in 2026, which is a major reason to choose Synology for long-term deployments.
 How much storage does a small business need?
 A typical 5 to 15-person small business needs 8TB to 24TB of usable NAS storage today, growing by 2TB to 10TB per year. A 4-bay NAS with 4x 8TB drives in RAID 5 (24TB usable) is a comfortable starting point. Plan for 3x your current footprint in three years and leave 20% headroom for snapshots and growth.
 Final Verdict: Which NAS Should Your Small Business Buy?
 The best NAS for small businesses in 2026 is the Synology DS1525+ for most teams, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus for budget-conscious buyers who want 10GbE, and the Synology DS225+ for the smallest teams that still want the DSM software experience. For 6-bay creative workflows, the UGREEN DXP6800 Pro is the strongest hardware pick. For rackmount deployments in a UniFi shop, the UNAS Pro 8 is the obvious choice. For VM hosting and ZFS, the QNAP TVS-h874-i5-32G is unmatched. For the most CPU and RAM per dollar, the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro is the deal of the roundup.
 Whichever unit you pick, pair it with CMR NAS-rated hard drives (WD Red Plus or Seagate IronWolf), a small UPS for graceful shutdowns during power events, and a 3-2-1 backup plan with one copy offsite. With those three things in place, your small business NAS will quietly serve your team for the better part of a decade.

 Frequently asked questions
 Do I actually need 10GbE?
 Only if you edit large photo or video files directly off the NAS, where it removes the network bottleneck. For backups, file sharing and streaming, 2.5GbE is genuinely plenty. The DXP4800 Plus builds 10GbE in and the DS923+ takes a card, so you can choose based on your workflow.
 What is the point of NVMe slots on a prosumer NAS?
 NVMe drives can act as a fast read or write cache to speed up busy workloads, or on supporting platforms run as a separate fast pool for active projects. They are most useful for editing, databases and many concurrent users rather than basic file storage and backups.
 Why does ECC memory appear on prosumer models?
 ECC corrects rare memory errors that could otherwise corrupt data, which power users handling important files value. The DS923+ and DS925+ include ECC, and the DXP4800 Plus uses ECC-grade DDR5. It is one of the features that separates prosumer boxes from basic home units.
 Can a prosumer NAS run virtual machines and containers?
 Yes, the Intel and Ryzen prosumer models with expandable memory handle containers and light virtual machines well, which is part of their appeal. Adding memory, up to 64GB on the DXP4800 Plus and 32GB on the DS923+, gives the headroom to run several services alongside your storage.
 Is UGREEN or Synology the better prosumer choice?
 It depends on what you weigh most. UGREEN offers the best hardware value, including built-in 10GbE on the DXP4800 Plus. Synology offers the best software with DSM, SHR and its app ecosystem, plus ECC and a 10GbE option on the DS923+. QNAP wins on sheer ports and connectivity.

 Most small businesses that own a NAS believe it's protecting them from more than it actually is. A box with two or four drives in RAID, sitting quietly in the server closet, feels like a solved problem — until a ransomware infection reaches the shared folder and encrypts every drive in the array at once, or a fire or break-in takes out the office and the "backup" sitting three feet from the workstation it was backing up.
 This guide is deliberately narrow: it's about the physical NAS hardware decision itself — which models make sense for a small business in 2026, what actually makes one ransomware-resistant versus just RAID-redundant, and how to combine it with cloud backup the right way. For the broader picture of business backup strategy — the 3-2-1 rule, Microsoft 365 backup gaps, and realistic Canadian cost ranges across every backup type — our cloud backup for business guide covers that ground in full. And if you're weighing NAS hardware against a fully managed backup service instead, our automated backups guide breaks down how that works and what it costs.
 Who wrote this guide
 This article was written and reviewed by IT Cares certified technicians based on selecting, configuring, and recovering NAS deployments for small businesses across Canada — including the calls that come in after a ransomware incident reached a NAS that had RAID but no immutable snapshots. We're not tied to one NAS brand — we're explaining what actually needs to be true about the hardware and configuration for it to protect a business when it matters.
 What Is a NAS, and Does Your Small Business Actually Need One?
 A NAS (Network Attached Storage) is a small dedicated storage server connected to your business network, with multiple bays to hold hard drives. Unlike a single external drive plugged into one computer, a NAS is reachable by every device on the network — Windows and Mac workstations, phones, tablets — and, configured correctly, from outside the office too.
 For a small business, the practical benefits are direct:
 Centralization — every company file lives in one place instead of scattered across eight different laptops
 RAID redundancy — if one physical drive fails, the data survives on the remaining drives
 Automatic workstation backup — every computer can back up to the NAS automatically (Time Machine for Mac, native Windows backup)
 Snapshots — point-in-time versions of your files you can roll back to in a few clicks
 Predictable cost — a one-time hardware purchase rather than a cloud subscription that climbs with every gigabyte added
 Secure remote access — remote employees reach the same files without relying entirely on a third-party service
 A NAS isn't the right fit for every business — if you'd rather keep everything in the cloud with no local hardware to manage, dedicated cloud backup covered in our automated backups guide may be the simpler path. But for a business handling meaningful file volume, local line-of-business software, or sensitive client data it wants direct control over, a NAS is usually the most cost-effective centerpiece of the setup.

 Before settling on a model, run it through this list. A NAS that checks every box actually protects you; one that checks half of them mostly delivers a false sense of security.
 Checklist: what to look for in a small business NAS
 At least 4 bays (2-bay models only make sense for a solo operator or a 1-2 person team)

 Immutable Snapshots: The Real Ransomware Defense
 This is probably the most important section of this guide, because it's where most small businesses get it wrong. RAID is not a backup. If ransomware infects a workstation connected to the NAS and starts encrypting files on the shared drive, RAID will faithfully replicate those encrypted files across every disk — RAID protects against hardware failure, not against corrupted or encrypted content.
 That's exactly the gap immutable snapshots close. A snapshot is a point-in-time photograph of your files. An immutable snapshot (sometimes called "locked" or WORM — Write Once, Read Many) cannot be modified or deleted for a period you define, even by a compromised administrator account.
 How this actually stops a ransomware attack
 The NAS takes automatic snapshots at regular intervals (hourly or several times a day) and locks them as immutable for, say, 14-30 days
 Ransomware infects a workstation and starts encrypting files it can reach, including those on the NAS's network share
 Active files on the NAS get encrypted — but the locked snapshots from previous days remain untouched, since even an administrator account can't modify them during the lock period
 The technical team isolates the network, cleans the infection, and restores files from the last clean snapshot — usually within hours rather than days or weeks
 On recent Synology models (DSM 7.2+), this feature is called Snapshot Replication with the immutable lock option, available on Btrfs-formatted volumes. QNAP offers similar protection on models supporting QuTS hero (ZFS file system) with locked snapshots. Always check the specific model's datasheet before assuming this is included — it isn't universal across every entry-level model, even within the same brand.
 Minimum recommended configuration
 For a small business, we recommend hourly automatic snapshots during business hours, locked in immutable mode for at least 14 days. That window covers the large majority of real-world scenarios: most ransomware infections are detected within days of landing, rarely more than two weeks later.
 Local vs Cloud vs Hybrid: An Honest Comparison for NAS Owners
 Even a local NAS with immutable snapshots stays vulnerable to one scenario: a fire, theft, flood, or physical disaster at the office destroys both your workstations and the NAS sitting right next to them. That's why real protection always combines a local component with an offsite one.

 The hybrid approach — a local NAS with immutable snapshots plus automatic, encrypted replication to a cloud service (Synology C2, Backblaze B2, or an equivalent provider) — is what we recommend to nearly all of our small business clients. In practice, that's the 3-2-1 rule applied concretely: your working copy (1), the local NAS (2, a different media type), and cloud replication (3, offsite). Our cloud backup for business guide covers the 3-2-1 rule in full depth if you want the broader picture beyond NAS hardware specifically.
 One important technical detail: cloud replication should use credentials separate from those used for day-to-day NAS access. If the same administrator account controls both the local NAS and the cloud copy, ransomware that compromises that account can potentially reach both. Always keep the access paths separate.
 Realistic Budget: What a NAS Actually Costs a Canadian Small Business
 The chassis is only part of the total cost. Here's a realistic breakdown by business size, in Canadian dollars.

In that context, the NAS is rarely the expense a small business regrets making.

 Case Studies: Three Canadian Small Businesses and Their NAS Choice
 These illustrative scenarios reflect situations we see regularly across small businesses in Canada, showing how these criteria translate into real decisions.
 Case 1: Accounting Firm in Ottawa (9 employees)
 The firm ran client files off a seven-year-old Windows file server with no snapshots and a manual backup to an external drive done "whenever someone remembered." After hearing about a nearby firm hit by ransomware during tax season, leadership decided to act. They chose a Synology DS1522+ with 5 drives in RAID 6, hourly immutable snapshots retained 21 days, and encrypted replication to Synology C2. Six months later, an employee clicked an infected attachment on a Friday afternoon. Ransomware encrypted files on their workstation and part of the network share before being caught Monday morning. Because the snapshots were immutable, the technical team restored every client file from a snapshot taken the day before the infection — the real loss was a few hours of one employee's work, not weeks of client records.
 Case 2: Dental Clinic in Burlington, Ontario (6 employees)
 A dental clinic handling patient records subject to health privacy obligations was using a consumer cloud service with no additional encryption and no control over where the data physically lived. During a compliance review, the clinic moved to an on-premises Synology DS423+ with AES-256 volume encryption, named-user access with two-factor authentication, and an encrypted offsite copy. This gave the clinic direct, documentable control over where and how patient data was protected — a concrete point in favor during their compliance review, alongside removing a growing dependency on an expensive high-volume cloud subscription.
 Case 3: Design Studio in Vancouver, BC (14 employees)
 The studio works with large files (video, high-resolution assets) that made pure cloud backup painfully slow on their standard business internet connection. The team chose a QNAP TS-464 with 16GB RAM for fast local editing over the network, regular ZFS snapshots, and scheduled overnight cloud replication so it wouldn't compete for bandwidth during working hours. The result: fast local access and backup for day-to-day work, with offsite protection quietly happening during off-peak hours.
 What all three have in common
 None of these businesses bought "the most expensive" or "the most powerful" NAS. Each chose a model sized to its actual data volume, legal obligations, and workflow — then invested in configuring immutable snapshots and offsite replication correctly. It's the configuration, not just the hardware, that determines whether a NAS actually protects a business.
 Deployment: The Steps That Actually Matter
 A brand-new NAS out of the box provides no real protection until it's configured correctly. Here's what a proper setup should cover.
 1
 Configure RAID for the drive count
 RAID 1 for two drives, RAID 5 or 6 for four or more (RAID 6 tolerates two simultaneous drive failures — recommended for businesses that can't afford extended downtime).
 2
 Turn on immutable snapshots
 Schedule automatic snapshots (typically hourly during business hours) and set an immutable lock period of 14-30 days.
 3
 Set up cloud replication with separate credentials
 Connect to the chosen cloud service using an account distinct from day-to-day access, with encryption enabled before data leaves the device.
 4
 User accounts and permissions
 One named account per employee (never a shared login), permissions restricted to what each role actually needs, two-factor authentication required for every administrator account.
 5
 Secure remote access
 A VPN or the manufacturer's secure access gateway rather than exposing the NAS directly to the internet — a common mistake that turns a NAS into an easy target for automated attacks.
 6
 Test a real restore
 Restore a sample file from a snapshot to confirm the whole chain genuinely works — not just in theory. Repeat this test quarterly.
 How long this takes: for a mid-size business, a complete, secured setup typically takes between half a day and two days depending on the complexity of the existing network and the volume of data being migrated.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is a NAS and does my small business actually need one?
 A NAS (Network Attached Storage) is a small dedicated storage server connected to your business network with multiple drive bays. It centralizes company files in one place, lets every workstation back up automatically, provides RAID redundancy against a single drive failure, and gives secure remote access without relying entirely on a monthly cloud subscription. For a small business handling client files, financial records, or other sensitive data, it's often the most cost-effective way to have real, direct control over your data.
 Is RAID on a NAS the same thing as a backup?
 No, and this is one of the most expensive misunderstandings in small business IT. RAID protects against a single physical drive failing — if one drive dies, the other still holds your data. RAID does not protect against ransomware (which encrypts files across every drive in the RAID volume at once), accidental deletion, or theft or fire at the office. RAID is an availability measure, not a backup strategy — it needs to be paired with immutable snapshots and an offsite copy.
 What is an immutable snapshot and why does it matter against ransomware?
 An immutable snapshot is a locked, point-in-time copy of your files that cannot be altered or deleted for a set retention period, even by an administrator account. This is the critical defense against ransomware: modern ransomware actively searches for connected shared folders and backups to encrypt them too, but it cannot touch snapshots locked in immutable mode. If your snapshots are immutable, ransomware can encrypt your active files, but a clean, untouched version from before the infection remains recoverable.
 How much does a NAS cost for a small business in Canada?
 A 2-bay NAS chassis alone runs roughly $250-$450 CAD, plus about $100-$180 CAD per NAS-rated hard drive. A 4-to-5-bay model with more RAM and immutable snapshot support typically runs $600-$1,100 CAD for the chassis, plus drives. Add roughly $10-$45 CAD per month for offsite cloud replication depending on volume. In total, a 10-to-25-employee business usually sets up a complete NAS solution — chassis, drives, and cloud backup included — for an initial budget of $1,500-$3,000 CAD, plus a modest recurring monthly cost.
 Should a small business use local NAS storage or cloud backup?
 It isn't a choice between the two — combining both is what actually provides real protection. A local NAS gives fast restores for everyday needs and doesn't depend on internet speed. A cloud copy protects against theft, fire, or flooding at the office since it's physically elsewhere. The hybrid approach — a local NAS with immutable snapshots plus an encrypted offsite cloud copy — is what genuinely satisfies the 3-2-1 backup rule, and it's what we recommend to the large majority of our small business clients.
 Synology or QNAP — which should a small business choose?
 Both are reliable brands used by thousands of small businesses. Synology (DSM) generally has a simpler interface, a strong reputation for stability, and solid immutable snapshot support on recent Btrfs-based models. QNAP (QTS or QuTS hero) often offers more raw performance and flexibility for a comparable price, with ZFS support on select higher-end models, at the cost of a somewhat more technical interface. For most small businesses without in-house IT staff, Synology is usually the simpler choice; for businesses with more demanding performance needs, QNAP is often the better value per dollar.
 How does a NAS fit into the 3-2-1 backup rule?
 The 3-2-1 rule requires three copies of your data, on two different media types, with one copy offsite. A properly configured NAS can cover two of those three requirements on its own: it's a different media type from the original workstation (copy 2), and with snapshot replication to a secondary NAS or the cloud, it can also provide the offsite copy (copy 3). In practice: workstation (copy 1) + local NAS with immutable snapshots (copy 2) + cloud replication of the NAS (copy 3) is a complete, proven 3-2-1 architecture for a small business.

 What to Look for in an NA for Small Businesses
 Key buying criteria so you get the right fit the first time.
 01 Remember every listed NAS here is diskless, budget drives separately
 The price shown for a NAS enclosure covers the hardware chassis, CPU, and RAM only, not the actual storage drives, NAS-grade drives built for 24/7 operation like Seagate IronWolf or WD Red still need to be budgeted on top, often adding $80 to $200 or more per bay depending on capacity and drive type.
 This matters because comparing NAS units purely by enclosure price without factoring in drive cost gives a misleading picture of the real total investment, a cheaper enclosure with more bays to fill can end up costing more overall than a pricier enclosure with fewer bays.
 Check whether a listing is diskless or ships with drives included, and add realistic per-bay drive costs to the enclosure price before comparing total cost across options.
 02 Weigh CPU class and RAM over bay count for real day-to-day performance
 Bay count determines maximum storage capacity, but CPU architecture (Intel, AMD, or ARM) and RAM amount determine how well the NAS actually handles real workloads, running apps, transcoding media on the fly, or serving multiple simultaneous users, and a higher bay count with a weak CPU can bottleneck performance regardless of how much raw storage it holds.
 This matters more the more the NAS will do beyond simple file storage, like Plex transcoding or running multiple docker containers, less if it's purely a basic backup target.
 Check the specific CPU model and RAM amount (and whether RAM is upgradeable) rather than choosing primarily by bay count.
 03 Understand RAID as a rebuild-time safety net, not a substitute for real backup
 RAID configurations protect against a single drive failure by letting the array rebuild from redundant data, but RAID is not a backup, it does nothing to protect against accidental deletion, ransomware, theft, fire, or a controller failure that affects the whole array at once.
 This distinction matters because treating RAID redundancy as sufficient backup protection is a common and risky misunderstanding, a real backup strategy needs a copy of critical data stored somewhere physically separate from the NAS itself.
 Check what RAID level a given NAS supports, and separately plan an actual backup strategy, ideally following a 3-2-1 approach, rather than relying on RAID redundancy alone.
 04 Match drive type (HDD vs SSD/NVMe) to your actual access pattern
 Traditional hard drives offer the lowest cost per terabyte for bulk storage like media libraries or backups, while SSD or NVMe-based NAS storage costs significantly more per terabyte but delivers much faster random access speeds, useful for frequently-accessed files, active project work, or serving as a fast cache tier.
 This matters directly based on how you'll actually use the storage, a media library accessed sequentially benefits little from SSD speed, while an active working file share benefits considerably.
 Check whether the NAS supports the drive type you need, and weigh the real cost-per-terabyte difference against how much you'll actually benefit from faster random access.
 05 Consider noise level if the NAS will run continuously in a shared living or office space
 A NAS that runs 24/7 generates continuous fan and drive noise, and that noise profile varies meaningfully between models, some use larger, slower-spinning fans that stay quiet, while others rely on smaller, faster fans that produce a persistent whine noticeable in a quiet room.
 This matters a great deal if the NAS will sit in a bedroom, living room, or shared home office rather than a dedicated closet or basement out of earshot.
 Check reviews specifically for real-world noise level mentions during continuous operation, not just idle noise, since drive activity and fan speed both increase under load.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 How many concurrent users can a small business NAS handle on gigabit Ethernet?
 A standard 1GbE connection works fine for document-heavy work with under 5 simultaneous users, but throughput per person drops noticeably once more people are transferring large files at the same time. 5GbE or 10GbE, on both the NAS and a matching switch, multiplies per-user throughput for larger or media-heavy teams.
 Do I need Active Directory integration for a small business NAS?
 Most small businesses eventually migrate from individual NAS logins to centralized directory sync as the team grows past roughly 5 users. It's useful for managing accounts at scale, but the setup is complex enough that it usually needs IT help to configure correctly the first time.
 Does the NAS itself need to be backed up?
 Most guidance treats a NAS only as a backup destination for computers, but ransomware attacks specifically targeting NAS devices are increasing. Set up cloud backup integration for the NAS's own data so a ransomware event or hardware failure doesn't destroy the only copy of your business files.
 Do I really need a UPS for a business NAS?
 Yes, treat it as a required companion purchase. A power outage that hits mid-write can corrupt a RAID array, and a USB-connected UPS lets the NAS detect the outage and shut down safely before that happens.
 What's the difference between Value-tier and Plus-tier NAS warranties?
 Value-tier models, like the Synology DS225+ or DS423 in this list, carry a shorter warranty with no enterprise support option. Plus-tier models, like the DS925+ or DS725+, offer longer coverage and an enterprise support add-on, worth the price step up for business-critical data.
 Should a small business start with a 2-bay or 4-bay NAS?
 If the team is small and unlikely to grow much, a 2-bay unit like the UGREEN DXP2800 covers the basics affordably. If growth is likely, either start with an expandable 2-bay unit like the Synology DS725+ or go straight to a 4-bay model like the DS925+ or UGREEN DXP4800 Plus to avoid a second purchase within a year or two.
